This is unlike semen, which is not property, and for this reason the Lawgiver forbade exchange involving it. The jurists agreed that if a stallion mounts a mare, the foal belongs to the owner of the mare.

(Section)

If it is asked: Can the fetus be formed from two waters and two men?

It is said: This is a legal and natural question, and the Law in it follows creation. Scholars have differed on it both legally and in terms of divine decree. A group rejected this and utterly refused it, saying: When the water settles in the womb, the womb encloses it and contracts around it to the utmost degree, so that no space the size of the mark of a needle's head remains open. It therefore cannot open after that to a second water, neither from the one who had intercourse nor from anyone else.

They said: It is on this basis that Allah has established the custom that a child can have only one father, just as a mother can be only one. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

Another group said: Rather, it can be formed from two or more waters. They said: The contraction of the womb and its enclosing of the water does not prevent it from receiving a second water, for the womb is the most eager and most receptive thing to semen.

They said: The example of this is like the stomach: when food settles in it, it contracts upon it to the utmost degree, but when more food reaches it, it opens to receive it because of its eagerness for it.

They said: This was testified to by a qa'if (one who identifies lineage by physical resemblance) in the presence of Amir al-Mu'minin Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning a child that two men claimed. He looked at them and at the child and said: "I do not see him except as having been produced by both of them." Umar agreed with him and attributed the child to both of them. Imam Ahmad and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them both, agreed with this.

They said: Sense perception witnesses to this, as you see in the puppies of a bitch and the kittens of a cat, which are born of varying colors because of the multiplicity of their fathers. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him not water with his semen the crop of another," meaning having intercourse with a pregnant woman by someone other than the one who impregnated her.

Imam Ahmad said: Intercourse increases the child's hearing and sight, and this is after conception.

If it is asked: Is it possible for two children to be formed from the water in one womb?

It is said: This is the question of twins, and it is possible; indeed, it has occurred. It has several causes. One is the abundance of semen, which flows into the womb in several surges. In the movement of the semen, the womb experiences various spasmodic movements, so it may happen that the attraction for the first surge of semen is on one side, and for the second, on the other side. Another cause is that the chamber of the children in the womb has compartments, so the semen is abundant, and one compartment may overlook some excess that is contained in the second compartment. And so on for a third. Aristotle said that a woman may carry five children in one womb. It is reported of a woman who gave birth in four deliveries to twenty children. The author of al-Qanun (Ibn Sina) said: I heard in Jurjan that a woman miscarried a sac containing seventy very small forms. Aristotle said: If a woman bears twins, a boy and a girl, rarely do the mother and the child survive. If she bears two boys or two girls, they often survive. He said: A woman may conceive upon a pregnancy, but usually the first dies. A woman once miscarried twelve fetuses, pregnancy upon pregnancy. As for when the pregnancy is single, or after the first has been delivered, both may survive. And Allah knows best.

If it is asked: What is the cause that generally prevents a pregnant woman from menstruating?

Imam Ahmad and Abu Hanifa said: What she sees of blood is blood of corruption, not menstruation. Al-Shafi'i, although he said it is menstrual blood, and this is one of the two reports from Aisha, there is no doubt that it is rare in comparison with the more common case.

It is said: Menstrual blood is divided into three parts. One part goes to the nourishment of the fetus. One part rises into the body. And one part is held back until the time of delivery, when it comes out with the child. This is postpartum bleeding (nifas). Sometimes the substance of the blood is strong and abundant, so some of it comes out because of its strength and abundance. The stronger evidence is that it is menstruation and has its ruling, since there is no rational or legal evidence preventing it from being menstruation. The full evidence from both sides we have mentioned in other places. And Allah knows best.

If it is asked: What is the reason that pregnant women, in the second and third months, crave to eat strange things that are not considered food by medicine?

It is said: When menstrual blood has been held back in them by a wisdom that Allah has decreed, namely that its diversion to the nourishment of the child is necessary, and the amount they need is small, the sound nature pushes it to the mouth of the stomach, and that produces in them the craving for those strange things.

If it is asked: How is the fetus positioned in its mother's womb: standing, sitting, or lying down?

It is said: It is supported by its face on its legs, with its palms on its knees, its legs folded toward its feet, and its face toward its mother's back. This is from the divine care, that He seated it in this position in the narrow place in the womb in this form. Also, if its head were downward, the weight of the lower organs would fall upon the noble organs, which would lead to its destruction. And when it attempts to come out, if it has turned, it helps it to come out, for when it emerges, the first thing to come out is its head, because when the head comes out first, the emergence of the other organs after it is easy. If it came out in another way, there would be obstruction and difficulty. For if the two legs came out first, the emergence of the rest would be obstructed. If one leg came out first, it would be obstructed at the second. If both legs came out together, it would be obstructed at the hands. If the two legs and the two hands came out, it would be obstructed at the head, which would twist backward, and the navel would twist toward the neck. The womb would then be in pain, delivery would be difficult, and it would lead to illness or death.

If it is asked: What is the cause of miscarriage, which they call tarh (expulsion), before the child is complete?

It is said: The fetus in the womb is like the fruit on the tree. Each of them has a strong connection to its source, which is why it is difficult to cut the fruit from the tree before it is complete, and it requires force. When the fruit reaches its full stage, it becomes easy to pick, and it may even fall by itself. This is because the ligaments and veins that draw from the tree were at their strongest and most nourishing. When that nourishment returns to the tree, those moisture channels weaken, and the weight of the fruit helps, so it is easy to take. It is similar with the fetus: as long as it is in the womb before it is complete and firm, its moisture and membranes prevent it from falling. When it is complete and mature, those moistures weaken, the membranes are torn, and the sliding moisture gathers, and the fetus falls. This is the natural course when the nature is upright and sound. Miscarriage before that happens because of a defect in the fetus, or a defect in the mother's nature, or the nature has weakened, just as fruit falls before it ripens because of a defect that arises, or because of weakness in the root, or a defect that arises from outside. So the miscarriage of a fetus is due to one of these three causes. The afflictions that strike fetuses are like the afflictions that strike fruits.

If it is asked: How can something much larger than the womb come out of it, given its narrowness?

It is said: This is among the greatest proofs of the care, power, and will of the Lord, Exalted is He. The womb must open to a very great extent. Many wise people have said that there must be a separation that befalls the great joints, which then close together more quickly than the blink of an eye. Skilled and learned physicians have acknowledged this and said: This cannot happen except by divine care and a management that the intellects cannot comprehend, and it compels acknowledgment of the perfect lordship and power of the Mighty Creator.

If it is asked: What is the cause of the infant's crying at the moment of its emergence into this world?

Ibn al-Qayyim, Tafsir (commentary on Surah 51, verse 21), part 7 of 15

The Creator, glory be to Him, secured the place of the liver and set it in position by binding it to the stomach and to all the intestines with veins, and with the membrane stretched over the abdomen that holds all of them together. He attached to it ligaments from every direction. Its binding membrane connects to the diaphragm (al-hijab) with a strong bond, and the ligament of the liver to the diaphragm is firm and secure, because the liver is suspended from it. The diaphragm is harder than the membrane of the liver, because there is great need for its hardness, since it protects the liver and the hollow vein (al-'irq al-ajwaf). Whenever a calamity befalls it, the animal dies, just as the branches of a tree perish when a calamity strikes its trunk.

He made the thinnest of these ligaments at the back, because it is firmly attached to the bones, and the thickest at the front, where there are no bones to protect it. This is part of the strength of the binding about which God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We created them and strengthened their frames﴾. He bound their joints with firm ligaments and made their creation joined one part to another.

Since the diaphragm is a noble instrument of the soul, it was given space from the two organs adjoining it, the stomach and the liver, in the measure of its need, so that they would not press upon it and hinder it from its function. Thus the stomach was kept away from it by the length of its passage.

(Section)

As for the spleen (al-tihal), some say that it has no benefit and that it was only placed to occupy the space so that it would not remain empty, lest one side of the body tilt because of the weight of the liver. So it was made to counterbalance the liver.

I say: this is wrong in one respect and right in another. As for what is right, it is among the marvellous wisdoms that the spleen was placed on the left side to balance the liver, so that the right side does not tilt because of it. The stomach cannot counterbalance the liver, because it is constantly filling and emptying: at times it is lighter than the liver and at other times heavier, so the body would sway or lean towards the side of the liver at one time and towards the side of the stomach at another. So the Creator, glory be to Him, made the spleen balance the liver and placed the stomach between them in the middle, so that one side does not become heavier and the other lighter when it fills and empties. Since it was made central, the posture of the body does not vary with its changes.

As for what is wrong, it is his saying that it has no benefit and only occupies space so that it does not remain empty. Even if no benefit is known in it, one may not deny that it has one, for lack of knowledge of a benefit is not knowledge of its absence. Nothing in the body is entirely without benefit. Among the spleen's benefits is that it draws from the liver the thick, turbid, black residue, by a type of vessel of the same kind as the veins, like a neck (ʿunuq) for it. When that residue reaches it, it cooks and transforms it, for it cooks thick and turbid blood, just as the colon cooks thick and dry food. In its function it uses the many arteries (al-ḍawārib) spread throughout it. What is cooked and transformed into its nature becomes nourishment for it, and what cannot be turned into blood suitable to it, it expels to the stomach by another neck of the same kind as the veins. It is able to draw the black excess with strength because of its fleshiness, for it is loose, yielding and light, like a sponge. Since the many arteries are joined to it, it is spared the need to cook the black humours, so that its flesh remains light and yielding, because the blood of the arteries (al-sharayīn) is thin, subtle, and close in nature to vapour. Whatever it is nourished by is slender, as is the lung. But the lung is nourished by what is pure, fine and bright, and red and fiery; likewise the lung is lighter in weight than it, more delicate in substance, and inclined to whiteness. As for the spleen, it is nourished by a subtle water from the black humour cooked in the arteries, whereby the body is relieved of it, and the spleen is nourished by it. So the spleen is nourished by a subtle nourishment from the nourishment of the liver, because it filters into it from the arteries that are pure. Each of them loves the other greatly. Because of the blackness of that residue and its turbid origin, the colour of the spleen was not red nor bright.

As for the liver, it is nourished by thick, surplus blood that filters into it from the veins other than the arteries. Because of the excellence of its nourishment its colour is red, and because of its surplus it is dense. So the liver is nourished by red, thick blood, the spleen by black, subtle blood, and the lung by pure, bright blood in the utmost state of maturity, close to the nature of the spirit. Thus the essence of each organ is as its nourishment, suited to it. The nourisher resembles the nourished in nature and function. This is as God's wisdom in His creation is manifest, so too His wisdom is manifest in His law and command, in that He forbade foul foods to His servants, for when they are nourished by them, they become part of them, and their parts come to resemble their foods, since the nourisher resembles the nourished, indeed it is transformed into its essence. For this reason the human species is the most balanced of the animal kinds in temperament, because its nourishment is balanced. Feeding on blood and the flesh of predators gives the one who feeds on them a satanic, predatory, aggressive power over people. So among the excellences of the Sharia is the prohibition of these foods and their like, except when a greater benefit opposes them, as in cases of necessity. For this reason, when the Christians ate pork, it produced in them a kind of coarseness and hardness. Likewise whoever eats the flesh of predators and dogs acquires something of their power. Since the satanic power is an inherent, constant and permanent trait of the fanged predators, the Lawgiver forbade them. Since the satanic power is an accidental trait in camels, he commanded that it be broken by ablution for whoever eats them. Since the nature of the donkey is inherent in the donkey, the Messenger of God forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys. Since blood is the vehicle and channel of Satan, God, exalted is He, forbade it with a binding prohibition.

Whoever reflects upon God's wisdom in His creation and command, and connects this with that, opens for himself a great door to knowledge of God, His names and His attributes. This is what moved us to expound at length on this subject, in which one rarely sees anything but one of two paths: the path of a physician who opposes revelation, imitating Hippocrates and his company, whose eye has passed over the messengers and what they brought, and who is among those of whom God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had, and there befell them what they used to mock﴾. And the path of one who denies all of that, rejects its speaker, and supposes it contradicts the Sharia, thereby denying God's wisdom in His creation and the excellence of His craftsmanship. Both paths are blameworthy, and whoever travels them is deprived of reaching the goal. So we do not deny the law of God, nor do we deny the wisdom of God. What corrupts people most is that they have seen only a naturalist (ṭabāʿī) heretic, detached from the sacred laws, or a lax one who disparages what God's wisdom and will have ordained in His creation, denying the powers, natures, causes, wisdoms and reasons. When the first wishes to enter Islam, the ignorance of these people and their obstinacy against both reason and the senses hinders him. When the second wishes to enter into knowledge of the wisdoms, ends, and the benefits, powers and causes that God has placed in His creatures, the heresy and unbelief of these people, their turning away from what the messengers brought, and their disparagement of the knowledge they possess hinder him. So he chooses his religion over his intellect, and he chooses, with his intellect, what has settled in him that neither his senses nor his reason obstinately deny, over religion. This has afflicted the people of medicine and the naturalists. For him, it is one of the kinds of evidence for tawhid, the return (al-maʿad), the attributes of the Creator, and what the messengers reported; indeed the messengers' reports are among its most manifest proofs, and the inner heart only increases in faith through it. What the messengers reported does not contradict what God's custom and wisdom in His creation have established, namely the setting up of causes and the ordering of their effects upon them, by His knowledge and wisdom. The source of His creation and command is His knowledge, exalted is He, and the blessings of the Lord, exalted is He, do not conflict, do not contradict one another, and do not nullify one another. And God knows best.

Section

The liver and the spleen face each other, and the stomach is between them. The stomach is joined to the arteries (al-ʿurūq al-ḍawārib). The heart is like the oven (al-tannūr) or like the furnace of the bath (ātūn al-ḥammām), which heats its water, and it has an opening to every room through which the heat of the fire passes into it. Likewise the innate heat (al-ḥarārah al-gharīziyyah), whose source is the heart, penetrates through channels and openings to all the organs and warms them.

(Section)

The organs were made a conveying passage. The stomach is the instrument for digesting food and assimilating it, and the intestines convey it to the liver. Since the intestines are the instrument of conveyance and connection, their coils and length were multiplied, and the veins that come to them from the liver are countless, so that the nourishment may pass into them gradually, first by first, and be released little by little. Had the coils of the intestines not been lengthened, it would have exited before taking its essence, and the appetite for food would have come upon them constantly, and the person would have lacked leisure for his welfare and his other affairs, and would have been constantly absorbed in food. For this reason, the animal that has no coils in its intestines, but a single straight intestine, is constantly absorbed in food and impatient to be without it, like the elephant. As for those whose intestines have coils, if the food, or part of it, leaves them in the first coil, it meets it in the second; if it misses it in the second, it meets it in the third, fourth and fifth in the same way. Thus the ability to endure without food is a profound wisdom. What reaches the intestines is drawn from the pulsing veins, and takes a small, subtle portion of the nourishment. As for the non-pulsing veins, they are truly the channels of nourishment, so they take most of it. The pulsing veins were made a passage for the spirits issuing from the heart, so they are sufficient with little nourishment. A connection to the intestines was made for the heart, so that it might first improve them and supply them with the strength of the innate heat by the permission of their Creator; then it takes from them the portion of nourishment suited to it, which is spared the function of the liver, because its substance is suited to the heart. For if this portion were to reach the liver, its burning and corruption would not be safe, and the heart would not benefit from it. Then it takes from them, at the time of great need and the sharpness of hunger, quickly, from the nearest places. This is why one who eats a strong broth (masnabah) is observed to feel an increase and growth in all his organs, even before the food settles in his stomach. Glory be to Him who perfected what He made.

Since the stomach is the instrument for digesting food and the intestines are the instrument for expelling it, two layers were made for the intestines, so that their expulsion is strengthened by both together, and as a protection and safeguard for them. For this reason, if an ulceration of the intestines occurs by the wearing away of one of the two membranes, the other remains intact. The thick intestines were made for expelling the residue, and the thin ones for the digestion of food. The reason that a person does not need to take food constantly is the multiplicity of the coils of his intestines, and the reason that prevents the constant expulsion of waste is the width of the thick intestines, which take the place of another vessel similar in width to the stomach, just as the bladder is a vessel for urine.

(Section)

We shall mention a brief section on this subject that gathers its scattered parts with clarity and conciseness, God willing, and power is from God. We say:

The oesophagus (al-marīʾ) is placed behind the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm) and along the spine, and it ends in its course at the diaphragm. It is bound by ligaments. When it moves away, it inclines to the left side and widens, and that widened part is the stomach. Its lower part returns inclining to the right. The stomach is the seat of its cooking, and its mouth is its upper opening, which they call the fuʾād (heart/fuʾād), and this is among their errors, unless it is a special terminology of theirs. Fuʾād, according to the lexicographers, is the heart. Al-Jawhari said: "al-fuʾād is the heart." Al-Asmaʿi said: "In the cavity is the fuʾād, which is the heart." Some lexicographers distinguished between the qalb and the fuʾād. Al-Layth said: "The qalb is a lump of the fuʾād, suspended by the nayāṭ (aorta)." A group said: "the opening of the heart." The Prophet ﷺ said: "The people of Yemen have come to you, more tender of hearts (araqq qulūban) and softer of hearts (alyan afʾidatan)." Thus he distinguished between them, describing the qalb with tenderness (ruqqah) and the afʾidah with softness (līn). As for the claim that the mouth of the stomach is the fuʾād, we know of no lexicographer who said this. Consider the Prophet's ﷺ description of the heart with ruqqah, which is the opposite of hardness and coarseness, and of the fuʾād with līn, which is the opposite of dryness and hardness. When the softness of the fuʾād is combined with the tenderness of the heart, mercy, compassion, kindness and the knowledge and acceptance of truth result. For softness brings about acceptance and understanding, and tenderness requires mercy and compassion, and this is knowledge and mercy, and by them a person's perfection is complete. Our Lord encompasses all things in mercy and knowledge. Let us return to what we are concerned with, and we say:

The stomach, together with the oesophagus, has two fine layers. The flesh in the inner layer is less, and therefore whiteness predominates in it; it is nervous and sensitive. In the outer layer the flesh is more, and therefore redness predominates in it. It is bound to the spine by firm ligaments. From its lower end it ends in an opening, which is the door of the stomach, and its gatekeeper (bawwāb) closes when it contains food during the period of its digestion. The inner substance of the stomach's body is called the velvet of the stomach (khamal al-maʿidah).

The intestines are the maṣārīn, the plural of miṣrān (with a dammah on the mīm), and it is the plural of maṣīr, and it was named maṣīr because the food arrives at it (maṣīr al-ghidhāʾ ilayhi). The lower ones are called al-aqtāb, and from it is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "the intestines of his belly will spill out" (fatandalaqa aqtābu baṭnihi).

The upper ones are thinner than the lower, for the wisdom mentioned earlier.

The uppermost of the thin intestines is called al-ithnā ʿashar (the twelve), because its measure is twelve fingers. Next is the one called al-ṣāʾim (the fasting one), because the food lingers little in it, not because it is ever found empty, as some have supposed, for this is false both by the senses and by the sacred law, as we shall mention. The third is called al-raqīq (the thin) and al-lafāʾif (the coiled), and it is the longest of the intestines and the most convoluted, and the food lingers longer in it; the veins that come to it from the liver are fewer. As for the two before it, they are set upright along the length of the body and are short, and the food lingers little in them; and in the fasting one it lingers least. These three are called the upper intestines and the thin intestines, and they are all within the width of the gatekeeper.

As for the ad-dāmiʿ (the lower one), the first of the three lower ones, it is called al-aʿwar (the blind), because it has no opening of its own; rather it is like a pouch, from which what entered comes out by the same way it entered. Its wisdom from God, glory be to Him, is that hard things that are difficult to digest are completed in it, as this is done in the gizzards of birds; and it is placed on the right side.

The fifth, called "they say," begins from the right side and takes a course across to the left, and in it the residue is retained, and it may sometimes exhaust what is in it.

The sixth is the last, and it is the straight intestine (al-maʿy al-mustaqīm), because it is straight in position along the length of the body. It is very wide, and the residue gathers in it just as urine gathers in the bladder, and upon it is the sphincter that prevents the residue from leaving without the will.

It is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The believer eats in one stomach, and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines." Here he applied the name "intestine" (maʿan) to the stomach by way of predominance, and because of its resemblance to the intestines, since each of the intestines and the stomach is a place for food. This is the usage of the Arabs, as they say al-qamarān (the two moons), al-ʿumarān (the two Umars), al-rukнān al-yamāniyān (the two Yemeni corners), al-shāmiyān and al-ʿIrāqiyān, and similar examples. Especially since the structure of the intestines is like the structure of the stomach, for it is composed of two layers, an outer fleshy layer and an inner nervous layer, and the inner layer has mucous linings connected to it to protect it from the heat, pain and foulness of the excrement; they are dense, so it does not grip it and nothing of it clings to them. Since the disbeliever has in his heart nothing of faith and goodness with which he is nourished, his powers and his appetite all turn to animal, bestial food, since he lacks spiritual, heart-nourishment. So his intestines and powers are devoted to this food, and his intestines empty it and fill themselves with it according to their readiness and receptivity, just as the veins and the stomach are filled with it. As for the believer, he eats only what sustains him, so that he may be strengthened for what he has been commanded. His aspiration and his powers are directed to matters beyond eating. When he eats what nourishes him and sustains his backbone, his heart, soul and spirit are satisfied with spiritual nourishment and need not multiply animal food. So he concentrates his one stomach on food, holding it until the organs and powers take from it the measure of their need, and he does not need to fill all his intestines with food. This is a matter known by experience. When the sources of faith and the knowledge of God, His names and attributes, love for Him and longing for His meeting become strong in the heart, the servant is spared much food and finds in them a strength exceeding the strength of animal food. If your nature is too dense to grasp this and you are far from it, then consider the state of joy and delight at the renewal of a great blessing, and your remaining for a period without food or drink while your strength is abundant and the blood shows in your complexion, nourished by happiness and gladness. Yet there is no comparison between that and the joy of the heart, its bliss, and the rejoicing of the spirit in His nearness, love and knowledge, as it has been said:

Her tales of your remembrance occupy her, distracting her from food and provision.

And the Prophet ﷺ said in the hadith agreed upon as authentic: "I spend the night with my Lord, who feeds me and gives me to drink."

And the Truthful, the Believed (ﷺ) spoke the truth, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. The purpose of food and drink is nourishment that sustains. When a person receives the higher and nobler and more beneficial of the two nourishments, how would it not suffice him in place of common food? We observe that animal nourishment overpowers spiritual nourishment of the heart until its judgment prevails and this nourishment is entirely diminished. So how would the nourishment of the body not diminish when the nourishment of the heart and spirit takes over and its judgment prevails? The Prophet (ﷺ) would remain for days without eating anything, yet he had the strength of thirty men, and he would go around to all his wives in one night, and they were nine women. And this Messiah, son of Mary, is alive and has not died, and his nourishment is of the kind of the nourishment of the angels. You see the sick person remain for many days without eating or drinking, because his soul is occupied with fighting the disease and repelling it, and because nature is satisfied with the remaining nourishment that is in the intestines and the stomach during the period of battle. When the battle lays down its burdens, you see the intensity of his need for food. The fearful, the lover, the joyful, the grieving, and the one whose thought has overtaken him, his soul does not demand any food, like one who is free of all that.

(Section)

The liver is a fleshy organ interlaced with thin and thick veins, and around the liver is a sensitive nervous membrane that encloses it and folds back over its covering. The liver is the origin of nourishment, and the organs of nourishment are its servants and helpers.

For man, since he is like an independent tree, there was made for him what takes the place of a flowing river at the roots of the tree, irrigating it. This is the intestines and the stomach, which are in the position of the spring, and the veins flow from them in the manner of irrigation channels. The veins of the liver connected to the intestines are in the position of the roots of the tree connected to the earth of the irrigation channel; they draw water from it and convey it to the tree and its branches, leaves, and fruits. These roots draw water from mud and moist soil, and likewise the veins of the liver draw the pure essence of water and its clear part from its turbidity and transform it into the nature of the organs, just as the roots of the tree do. The shape of the liver is crescent-like, convex on its outer surface and concave on its inner surface, and it lies beneath the five ribs. It has five lobes called the extensions, which enclose the stomach just as the palm encloses the object grasped in its fingers. The small lobe in particular is called the liver's appendix (zā'idat al-kabd). In the authentic report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seventy thousand of the people of Paradise will eat from the extra part of the liver of the fish, which is their food." This indicates the great status of this appendix, so what is to be thought of the liver of which it is the appendix, and how of the fish that contains it?

Its concave side is called al-mawrid (the entry point), because it brings in nourishment from the stomach and the intestines, and it is called the gate of the liver. Then these veins branch out from its two sides into branches connected to the intestines, and these are called al-jadāwil (the channels), due to their resemblance to small irrigation channels, and they lead to a great hollow. These channels have membranes above and below them, so the veins connected to them encircle the intestines together, and these membranes and what they contain are called al-marābiṭ (the binders).

(Section)

The second vein divides at its draw into small veins, and smaller than those, until it reaches the utmost thinness; then it returns and gathers gradually, in proportion to how it was divided, taking from multiplicity to unity and from thinness to thickness, until there gathers from them the vein that comes out of the liver, called al-ajwaf (the hollow vein), and through it the blood is conveyed to the whole body. When it comes out, it divides into two parts. One of them takes its course through the diaphragm toward the heart, and it is called al-waṭīn (the aorta/main artery). The lexicographers said: al-waṭīn is a vein that waters the heart. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-waṭīn is a vein in the heart; if it is severed, its owner dies, and his waṭīn is struck, so he is mawtūn. Al-Wāḥidī said: al-waṭīn is the cord of the heart, a vein running along the back until it connects to the heart; if it is severed, the powers are nullified and its owner dies. This is the statement of all the lexicographers, and they recited for al-Shammākh:

"When it reaches me and I load my saddle upon her, ʿArāba, then you will gush with the blood of the waṭīn."

Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority of the exegetes said it is the cord of the heart and its tendon. As for al-abhar, about which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is the time for the severing of my abhar," al-Jawhari said: al-abhar is a vein, and if it is severed its owner dies. There are two abhars that come out of the heart, and then all the arteries branch from them. They recited for al-Asmaʿī:

"And for the heart there is a throbbing at its abhar, like the throbbing of the boy's blood behind the cover of the stone."

(Section)

The gall bladder is placed upon the liver and has two channels. One of them is connected to the concavity of the liver and draws the yellow bile, and the other is connected to the upper intestines and pours into the bile to wash and polish it. From it the secretion (al-sirr) extends to the bottom of the stomach to mix with the food, so that there is assistance in its digestion.

(Section)

The power that God, glorified and exalted, has entrusted with the management of the body is among the greatest of His signs that point to Him, for it performs on the food and drink that come to it varied actions: cutting, separating, rubbing, dissolving, and composing. The beginning of this is in the mouth, where it is cut by the teeth, chewed, and mixed with the moisture within it, and it is fully digested there. Then, upon its arrival at the stomach, it digests it again with another digestion, which is called the first digestion. The organs adjacent to it assist it in its digestion: the liver is on its right, the spleen on its left, the heart above it, the esophagus in front of it. The intestines are the passages that lead to it, and the veins are the routes that proceed from it. The innate heat is the fire that cooks the food within it, and the digestive, attractive, nutritive, and expulsive powers are its servants. When the food is digested within it, it becomes chyle (kīlūs), resembling thick barley water. Then its thick and fine parts are separated, and the thin veins, which are as fine as hair, expel the fine part, and it is drawn to the liver. When this fine part reaches the liver, the liver embraces all of it, cooks it, digests it, transforms it into its own substance, and turns it into blood; this is called the second digestion. Since this maturing and cooking resembles the cooking of a pot, something like foam and cream rises on it, which is yellow bile, and some sediment settles like dregs, which is black bile, and some part that has not fully matured and remains in its rawness is left behind, which is phlegm. The part that is clarified and remains from all of this is the blood, which is discharged from the liver through the great vein known as al-ajwaf, after its watery part has been separated out toward the organ of urine. This blood then travels through the veins branching from the hollow, then into perforated channels from the veins, then into perforated irrigation channels from the channels, then into suckers derived from the irrigation channels, then into thin hair-like veins, and then it seeps from their mouths into the organs so that they may be nourished by it. The organs then dissolve it and transform it into their substance, so that in the flesh it becomes flesh, in the bone bone, in the sinew sinew, in the nail nail, in the hair hair, and in the hearing, sight, and the organs of sense likewise. Blessed is He who made this from a drop of worthless water.

(Section)

Blood is the original mixture and the true nourishment of the body, and it replaces what decreases and dissolves from it. The other humours, such as spices and condiments, are of two kinds: one is subtle, which is the blood of the heart, and the other is thick, which is the blood of the liver. Its likeness is that of a ruler who is dignified, forbearing, and calm, by whom his subjects live; but when he becomes angry and enraged, he kills.

(Section)

As for phlegm, it is a crude, unripe, and soft humour that completes its maturation when nourishment is scarce, when the innate heat takes it, digests it, and turns it into blood. It is found in the stomach and the intestines, and in the liver when digestion is deficient. Among its benefits is that it moistens the body and lubricates the joints so that their movements are smooth, and it mixes with the blood in the nourishment of the phlegmatic-natured organs, such as the brain. Since the organs need it to be near them to moisten them, no organ was made specifically for it, especially since the organs are nourished by it when nourishment is lacking.

(Section)

As for yellow bile, it is a subtle, hot humour. The body's need for it is that it mixes with the blood, thins it with its subtlety, and carries it through narrow passages, and that it assists the blood in nourishing the hot and dry organs. What separates from them, of what they have no need, is filtered into the gall bladder to take its share from it, and what the gall bladder has no need of, it pours into the intestines to wash them from the stain of the dregs and their viscosity, and to release the sphincter of the anus so that one feels the need to defecate.

(Section)

As for black bile, it is a cold, dry humour. Among its benefits is that it travels with the blood through the veins to strengthen and fortify it, to hold it together, to keep it, and to prevent it from easily dissolving when needed. It assists in nourishing the organs that require some black bile in their nourishment, such as the bones. What joins them, and what they have no need of, is filtered to the spleen, and the spleen filters it thoroughly and nourishes itself by it. Then the spleen sends what it has no need of to the mouth of the stomach, where it tickles it with the sourness it contains, so that appetite is stirred and one feels hunger. Then the outer organs seek their known portion and share from the organs adjacent to them, and the adjacent organs seek it from those next to them, and so on until the demand reaches the stomach. Hunger is the demand of the outermost organs upon the lowest organs.

(Section)

Since the wisdom of the Lord, majestic in His majesty and sanctified in His names, there is no god but Him, decreed that the human body, in its conditions, is likened to a city, there should be found in it principal organs that manage its affairs, just as the leaders of the city manage its affairs, and that they hold the position of governors and rulers; and organs that serve these principal organs, for the chief cannot be a chief without a subordinate, and these are like the police, the enforcers, and the chiefs of the quarters. There should also be found in it organs like the subjects, and they are of two kinds: those that are connected to the leaders by service, and those that have no connection with them but are independent in themselves. Accordingly, by this division, the organs are four: the first, the principal served organs; the second, the subordinate serving organs; the third, the subordinate organs without service; and the fourth, the organs that are neither principal nor subordinate.

(Section)

The principal organs deserve leadership because of their nobility, since they are the origins, sources, and beginnings of the primary powers in the body, which are necessary for the survival of the individual and the species. By the survival of the individual they are three: the heart, the liver, and the brain; and by the survival of the species they are four: the three mentioned and the two testicles. As for the heart, it is what the Creator, the All-Knowing, made to stand over the affair of the body as the king stands over his subjects. It is the first organ to move in the body and the last organ to become still, and it is the origin of all creation; whatever good or corruption befalls it, its effect extends from it to the other organs.

As for the liver, it is the organ that stands for the preservation of life, since it is what fills the organs with nourishment so that the body may remain preserved as long as its survival is possible.

As for the brain, it is the organ that stands over sensation and perception and the perfection of life, since in it are the instruments of sensation by which one knows the beneficial from the harmful and the agreeable from the disagreeable, and by it life becomes beneficial, wholesome, and surpassing the mere adornment of plant life.

As for the two testicles, they are the two that stand for the preservation of the species.

(Section)

As for the subordinate organs, such as the lungs and the arteries that carry from the heart the innate heat, the powers, and the animal spirits (al-arwāḥ al-ḥayawāniyya), by which the body subsists, these two serve the heart. The stomach and the veins serve the liver; the veins convey the nutritive blood and the powers to the whole body. The liver serves the brain. Likewise the nerves, by which sensation and movement occur. The two testicles are served by the organs that convey the seminal fluid and the channels that conduct it to the places of procreation.

(Section)

As for the subordinate organs without service, they are organs distinguished by powers that have a nature by which their management is completed and their affairs are made upright. This does not preclude that powers are drawn to them from the principal organs, by God's permission, such as the ear, the eye, and the nose; for each of these manages its own affairs by the natural power that the Creator, glorified be He, gave it, and this cannot be completed except by a sensory power coming down to it from the brain, by God's permission.

(Section)

As for the organs that are neither principal nor subordinate, they are those distinguished by innate powers that they have from the origin of creation at the beginning of formation, so that by them the affairs of these organs are upheld and managed, in bringing benefits and repelling harms. Such are the bones, the cartilage, and the rest of the organs of uniform parts, like the ligaments, the sinews, the tendons, the arteries, the veins, the membranes, and the flesh, and the bones are like the foundations and pillars for building the framework of the body.

If it is said: Is there in the bones the power of sensation and its life or not? It is said: This is a matter on which the scholars of the Law differ among themselves, and the scholars of medicine differ among themselves. One group said: there is no life in the bones, although there is in them the power of growth and nourishment. They said: life is only the animal spirit, and the bones have no share in it. They said: the vehicle of life is only the blood spread through the veins, the nerves, and the flesh; for this reason the hair and the nail have no share of it, and for this reason a person does not feel pain when they are cut. They said: the life of the bones and the hair is a life of growth and nourishment, and the life of the organs of the body is a life of growth and sensation. They said: For this reason we say that bones do not become impure by death, because there was no life in them that departs with death. They said: The cessation of growth does not necessitate the impurity of what has departed from it, as the evidence of the drying of crops and trees shows.

Others said: The proof that bones are animated by life is the words of the Most High: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ Say: ﴿He will give them life who produced them the first time.﴾ Sensation also indicates this, for the bone feels pain, is struck, and becomes still, and that is the very perception of it. They said: It is not possible to deny that the bones have a sensory power that feels cold and heat.

The others said: Sensation and pain belong not to the bone in itself but to the flesh adjacent to it.

Their opponents said: This is manifest obstinacy, for the bone itself feels pain, especially when it is broken. Furthermore, the teeth and molars feel hot and cold pain by themselves, not by the flesh adjacent to them. For this reason a third group took a middle position and said: The bones of the teeth in particular have sensation, unlike the rest of the bones. These have conceded the question from a near place, for what indicates the sensation and life of the teeth is the same as what indicates the life of the rest of the bones, and the doubt they have raised, if it were valid, would prevent the sensation of the teeth.

As for the hadith on purity and impurity, that is for another reason beyond life. Whoever deems them impure by death equates them with flesh; and whoever does not deem them impure, which is the stronger position in evidence, does so because the cause of impurity is absent in them, and death is not the cause of impurity; it is only an indication of the cause and its occasion. The cause is the retention of waste matter in the flesh and the bone, and the bone is free of that. The evidence for this is that the Lawgiver did not rule the impurity of the living creature that has no flowing blood (nafs sā'ila) because waste matter is not retained in it. So it is more fitting and more worthy that the bone should not be ruled impure. For the moisture in the fly, the scorpion, and the beetle is greater than the moisture in the bone.

(Section)

As for the bones in the body counted by those who dissected, they are two hundred and forty-eight bones, apart from the small sesamoid bones that secure the joints of the fingers and those in the larynx. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that man was created with three hundred and sixty joints. If the joints are the bones, then Galen and others have acknowledged that there are small bones in the body that did not fall under their enumeration and counting. If the meaning of the joints is the places where the organs separate from one another, as al-Jawhari and others said, "the joint (mafṣil) is the articulation of the organs' joints," then that is more general than the bones, so consider it. As for the salāmiyyāt (phalanges/joints) mentioned in the hadith related by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ from the hadith of Abū Dharr: "Every joint (salāmā) of one of you has a charity due upon it; every tasbīḥa is a charity, every taḥmīda is a charity, every tahlīla is a charity, every takbīra is a charity..." the hadith. The salāmā is a bone, and its plural is salāmiyyāt. Thus there are three matters here: organs, bones, and joints.

God, glorified be He, made the bones the hardest thing in the body, so that they might be a foundation and a pillar in the body, since all the organs are placed upon the bones, even the heart, as its explanation will come, God willing. The bones carry the organs, and what carries is stronger than what is carried.

They are also for protection and shielding, like the skull, which is the protection of the brain, and the bones of the chest are a protection for it.

The bones were made to have many benefits and numerous advantages. Among them is movement, for a person may need the movement of some of his parts without others, and he may need the movement of part of an organ. Among them is that if it were on a single bone, when he wished to move, the whole would move together. Among them is that crafts and the loosening and binding of things would be impossible for him. Among them is that if a calamity afflicted one of them, it would spread to the whole body; so the bones were made numerous, so that when one of them is struck by a calamity, it does not spread to another, and the other bones stand in its place in securing that benefit. Among them is that the benefits that come from the multiplicity of bones would be lost; had they not been many and varied, those benefits would have been forfeited.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 51, verse 21 (part 9 of 15):

Among the wonders is that the body needs some bones to be large, some to be small, some to be elongated, some to be hollow, some to be curved, and some to be straight. None of this would be achieved without the multiplicity of bones.

Among them are the wondrous craftsmanship, the excellent arrangement, the assembly and the composition, and other benefits.

Then the Creator bound some of them to others with ligaments and a firm fastening. Then He clothed them with flesh, to guard and protect them. Then He clothed the flesh with skin, to preserve it.

Since waste matter is divided into fine and coarse, Allah, glorified is He, made for the coarse waste channels through which it is drawn downward and exits the body in a manner apparent to the senses. As for the fine waste, it is vaporous waste. Since its nature is to rise upward and leave the body through dissolution, He placed in the upper bones outlets through which the rising vapour dissolves. Those outlets were not perceptible, lest the shell of the brain, which is the skull (qahf), be weakened by harmful substances reaching it. So He made the brain enclosed by many bones and joined some of them to others by a joining called the shu'un (sutures). From this comes the saying of people: "So-and-so has not gathered the sutures of his head." The head, with all its parts, includes fifty-nine bones. He made the skull perfectly round at its front, its back and its sides, like the lid of a pot. Its bones are six: the bone of the crown (yafukh), the bone of the forehead, the bone of the back of the head, the two bones in which are the openings of hearing, and in each of the two temples are two solid bones.

The bones of the upper jaw are fourteen: six of them are in the sockets of the two eyes, two for the nose, two beneath the nose, which are the ones pierced toward the mouth, two in the cheeks, and two beneath the upper lip.

As for the bone resembling a peg, it is one, and it is like the base of the head.

The bones of the lower jaw are two, and they are joined at the middle of the chin, with a structure between them; and they connect above with the upper jaw by a hinged joint.

The teeth are thirty-two, in each jaw sixteen: four incisors, followed by the canines (rubā'iyyāt), followed by the eyeteeth (al-nābān), followed by the molars (al-adrās), five on this side and five on that side. The wisdom teeth (al-nawājidh) are the last of the molars; there are two wisdom teeth on each side, one on each side, and sometimes the wisdom teeth are missing in some individuals, and each side had four molars.

Allah has entrusted a person's food to his hand: the hand takes it and delivers it to his lips; the lips deliver it to the canines and incisors, which separate it; then it delivers it to the molars, which grind it; then it delivers it to the tongue and the mouth, which knead it; then it delivers it to the throat (ḥulqūm) and the gullet (marī'), which deliver it and convey it to the stomach. The stomach cooks it, ripens it and sets it right as it should be; then it delivers it to the liver, which makes it into blood, then sends from it to every organ its portion and allotted share. Then the bile's vessel pours into the black bile, into the spleen, and the residue is expelled from it as explained earlier.

(Section)

The head is used in a general sense for what the neck carries in its entirety, and in a specific sense for the scalp, which is the skin of the head where hair grows. The skull (jumjumah) is the bone that contains the brain, and it is composed of seven opposing pieces called the qabā'il (plates), and the places of their joining are called shu'un (sutures). The middle of the skull is called the hāmah (crown), and the limits of the hāmah on both sides are the horn of the head (qarn al-ra's); its limit at the front is the yāfukh, and at the back is the qamḥadwah, which is the part of the head of one lying on his back that touches the ground. It has three boundaries: the nuqrat al-qafā (the hollow at the nape), and the qadhālān (the two bony ridges), for the nuqrat al-qafā is its boundary from the rear of the middle, and the qadhālān are the two sides of the hollow. The detail of the seven plates has already been explained.

The skull is covered by the al-simḥāq (periosteum), which has two membranes in the middle: one that follows the skull, which is the thicker and harder of the two, and the other that encloses the brain, surrounds it and mingles with it. Each of them is called umm al-dimāgh (mother of the brain), and they are called al-amān (the two protectors). From this comes al-āmmah, and al-ma'mūmah, in which there is one third of the blood-money (diyya), which is the wound that reaches the umm al-dimāgh. It is called tajwīf al-dimāgh (the cavity of the brain).

And the brain has three ventricles (buṭūn). Between the two ventricles at its rear and middle there is a passage containing a piece of the brain, elongated and resembling a worm (dūdah); this passage is blocked and opened by it. Beneath the brain is an extended, spread-out plexus (sabalah) composed of pulsating veins, from which is generated a psychic spirit (rūḥ nafsānī) that passes into the two ventricles at the front of the brain.

In the brain are the basin (birkah), the reservoir (ḥawḍ), the funnel (qam'), the worm (dūdah), the ventricles (biṭān), the membranes, and the origins of the nerves. The brain contains three chambers, some passing through others, and they are called ventricles: the first at the front, which divides into two parts; the second in its middle; and the third at its rear. The substance of the brain is marrow-like in form, like a mail-shirt (zard) assembled together, and the psychic spirit is fixed in the gaps of the mail. The brain is divided lengthwise into two joined halves, and the division at the front of the brain is more apparent. The two membranes enter into the folds of the brain and its mail-like structure; the harder of them enters the ventricles between the two parts of the front ventricle and separates them; beneath it is a clarified reservoir called al-mu'ṣarah (the press), which pours the ripened blood into the veins and sends out streams that irrigate the front ventricle, and gathers into two large veins that carry the blood to the middle and rear ventricles. The middle ventricle is like a vestibule and a passage between the front and rear; its roof is vaulted like an arch. The brain is placed lengthwise over two closely adjacent projections, which touch and separate in the manner of opening, so the vestibule opens and the front and rear ventricles become visible. The rear part is less rounded than the front and smaller in its mail structure; it is elongated in shape and narrows gradually until the marrow flows from it like a stream from a spring.

In the brain there are two channels: one at the rear of the front and the middle, for the expulsion of its waste, and the two meet at one deep single outlet; the first is in the thin membrane and the other in the hard membrane, narrowing like a funnel.

Since the brain is the origin of the body's movements according to its will, and it has no need of strong motion, it was enclosed by a wall of bones, unlike the stomach, the liver, the womb, and all the organs of nutrition, which need to expand and fill with food, to be carried again and again, and to squeeze out and expel the waste. Bone would prevent this, while the joining alone suffices for the brain; so it was enclosed by a wall of bone.

As for the chest, since it needed firmness through bones and movement through joints, it was formed from both; and the belly is wider than the chest because of the nutritional organs lodged in it, the breathing apparatus, the spleen, the gullet and others.

(Section)

Now turn your attention to yourself and consider the first beginning: the drop of sperm, a base and weak droplet which, if left for an hour, would perish and spoil. How the Lord of lords brought it out from between the loins and the ribs; how He placed love and affection between males and females; then how He led them by the chain of love and desire to union; then how He extracted the sperm from the male through the motion of intercourse from the depths of the veins, and gathered it in the womb in a secure place which no hand can reach, no sun can look upon, and no air touches. Then He turned that sperm stage after stage and layer after layer, and nourished it with the water of menstruation.

And how did He, glorified is He, turn the sperm, which is white and bright, into a red clot, then made it a lump of flesh, then divided the parts of the lump into bones, nerves, veins, sinews and flesh, within the womb, in the three darknesses. Had the veil been lifted from you, you would have seen the design and the shaping appearing in that sperm, bit by bit, without your seeing the Shaper, His tool or His pen. Have you ever seen a craftsman whose tool you cannot sense or touch?

Then reflect on this great dome that has been set upon the two shoulders, and on what wonders have been deposited in it, what storehouses have been built into it, what benefits have been placed in those storehouses, and what this dome contains of bones of various shapes, qualities and benefits, and of fluids, nerves, paths, channels, the brain, the openings, and the inner powers of memory, thought, imagination and retention. In it are the power of reflection, the power of recollection, the power of imagination and the power of retention. These powers are deposited in their storehouse, subjected to serve its interests; it employs and uses them as it wishes.

Consider how He, glorified is He, shaped the head, and split its hearing, its sight, its nose and its mouth; and how He formed its sphere in the mother's womb from twenty-three bones, and created those bones in various configurations. Consider how that soft, weak sperm was transformed into hard, strong bones.

Then consider how He, glorified is He, determined each of those bones with a specific shape, such that from their totality arose what, had it been otherwise, would have destroyed the benefit and defeated the purpose; then He assembled some of them with others so that from their totality arose the sphere of the head in this particular form.

Since the head is the noblest of the human organs and the most comprehensive of the powers, benefits, tools and storehouses, divine providence required that it be protected with various kinds of safeguards. The brain is surrounded by a thin membrane, and above that membrane is another membrane called al-simḥāq; above that is a fleshy layer; above that fleshy layer is the skin; and above the skin is the hair. Thus Allah created above your brain seven layers, just as He created above the earth seven heavens in layers. The purpose of creating them is precaution in guarding the brain against afflictions. The brain within the head is like the heart within the body. He, glorified is He, divided it lengthwise into three parts: He made the front part the locus of retention and imagination; the middle ventricle the locus of contemplation and reflection; and the last ventricle the locus of recollection and recall of what one had forgotten. Each of these three functions is an important matter for a person, and he cannot do without it, for he needs understanding and explanation. Had he not been retentive of the meanings of concepts and their forms after their absence, then whenever he heard a word and understood it, it would vanish from him upon the arrival of the next, and the purpose of understanding and conveying would not be achieved. So his Lord and Originator provided him with a storehouse to preserve for him the forms of what is known, until they are gathered together for him; this faculty is called the retentive faculty, and a person's welfare is not complete without it. For when he sees a thing, then it is absent from him, then he sees it again, he knows that what he now sees is what he saw before, because in the first instance its form was fixed in the retentive faculty, then it was hidden from him by the veil; when he saw it a second time, this sensed form corresponded to the mental form in the mind, and certainty arose that this is that. Were it not for the retentive faculty, that would not have occurred, and a person would not recognize anyone after being absent from him. That is why, when the absence is very long and that first form has been completely effaced from the mind, the knowledge that this is the one he saw first does not arise except after reflection and contemplation.

Some have said that the locus of these forms is the soul (nafs); others said the locus is the heart; others said the locus is the intellect (ʿaql).

Each party has its proofs and arguments, and each has perceived something while missing something else, since the aforementioned perception depends on all of that together and is not complete without it.

The verified view is that the origin and source of all this is the heart, and its终 end and seat is in the head. This is the question on which the jurists differed: whether the intellect is in the heart or in the brain, on two opinions, two narrations from Imam Aḥmad having been related.

The verified view is that its root and substance is the heart, and it extends to the brain. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they might have hearts to understand with, or ears to hear with?﴾

Thus He placed the intellect in the heart, just as He placed hearing in the ear and sight in the eye. And Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾. More than one of the early scholars said: for whoever has intellect.

Others argued that a man is struck on his head and his intellect disappears, and that had the intellect not been in the head it would not have disappeared; for hearing and sight do not disappear by a blow to the hand or foot, nor by a blow to any other organ, because they are not connected to them. The proponents of the heart answered that its disappearance by the corruption of the brain is not impossible even if it is in the heart, because of the connection between the heart and the head; just as the growth of beard hair is not impossible after cutting off the testicles, and the corruption of a power by the corruption of an organ may occur because that organ is its locus and is connected to it. And Allah knows best.

In any case, this is among the greatest of Allah's signs, proofs, power and wisdom: how the image of the heavens and the earth, the seas, the sun, the moon, the climes, the kingdoms and the nations is imprinted in this small locus. A person memorizes very many books, various sciences and diverse crafts, and all of them are imprinted in this small part without any of these images mixing with others; rather, each image is established in this locus by itself. Yet if you tried to engrave many images and shapes in a small place, some would mix with others and obliterate one another; whereas in this small part, many different and even contrary images are engraved, and not one image cancels another.

Among the most wondrous things is that this intellectual faculty receives what the senses convey to it, gathering it together, and then each sense lends the benefit of the other sense. For example, you see a person and know that he is so-and-so; you hear his voice and know that it is him; you touch a thing and recognize it; you smell it and know that it is it. Then you infer from the voice you hear that he is the one you saw, so that hearing his voice suffices you from seeing him and takes the place of observing him. For this reason, most jurists permitted the testimony of a blind man, and his buying and selling, and they agreed on the permissibility of his having intercourse with his wife, though he has never seen her, relying on her voice. Indeed, even if she were mute and he deaf, it would be permissible for him to have intercourse with her.

Allah, glorified is He, has placed between hearing, sight and the heart a connection, a bond and an interplay by which one can take the place of another. For this reason He frequently mentions them together in His Book, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart—each of those will be questioned about﴾, and His saying: ﴿And We made for them hearing, sights and hearts﴾, and His saying: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾.

This is from the Creator's, glorified is He, care for the perfection of this human form, so that each sense takes the place of the other and serves its function in general, though not in everything.

Then Allah, glorified is He, deposited the power of reflection and commanded its use in what brings benefit to him in this world and the Hereafter. He composed the faculty of thought from two of the present things held by the retentive faculty, in a special composition; so from between these two things a third, new thing arises, of which the intellect had no awareness, though its materials were with it; but through the composition the third matter came about for it. From here arises the extraction of crafts, trades and sciences, the building of cities and dwellings, agriculture, farming, and other things. When the faculty of thought extracts this and finds it good, it hands it over to the active, knowing faculty, which transfers it from the register of minds to the register of concrete realities; so it was a mental matter, then became external existence. Were it not for reflection, a person would not be guided to obtain benefits and repel harms; and this is among the greatest blessings and the completion of divine care. That is why, when beasts and madmen and the like lack this faculty, they cannot attain what the people of thought attain.

Since extracting the sought-after object by this path involves thinking and estimating, one reflects first in extracting the material, then measures and divides it second, just as a tailor produces a garment and then measures and cuts it second.

Allah, the Exalted, says concerning [al-Walid]: ﴿Leave me with him whom I created alone, and to whom I gave vast wealth, and sons present with him, and smoothed for him the way smoothly. Then he desires that I should add more. No! Indeed he has been stubborn toward Our signs. I will impose upon him a grievous ascent. Indeed he reflected and calculated, so may he be destroyed, how he calculated! Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾

So He repeated the word "calculated" without "reflected," and condemned him for it without reflection. This is set down according to the requirement of the situation, for by reflection one seeks to extract the unknown, and that is not blameworthy; but once he has extracted it, he makes two calculations: a general calculation and a particular calculation.

The general calculation is that the sorcerer is the one who separates a man from his wife. The particular calculation is that the one who separates a man from his wife is blameworthy. Here, then, is one calculation after another, and for this reason He repeated it and condemned him for it.

As for reflection, it seeks knowledge of a thing, so it is not blameworthy; unlike one who, after his reflection, calculates what leads him to establish falsehood and nullify truth. So consider this well.

(Section)

Then descend to the eye, and contemplate its wonders, its shape, its creation, the placement of the seeing light within it, and its composition of ten layers and three humours.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 51, verse 21 (part 10 of 15):

Each of these layers and humours has a specific shape and a specific size. Were it not so, the intended benefit would be disrupted. He, glorified is He, placed the place of sight in the size of the lens, then displayed within that lens the size of the heavens, the earth, the mountains, the seas, the sun and the moon. Consider how that lens is wide enough for things to be imprinted in it, though they have no comparison to it whatsoever. He placed that seeing faculty in a black part. So reflect on how the seer is sustained by this black part.

He, glorified is He, made the pupil (al-hadaqah) protected by the eyelids, to cover it, preserve it, polish it, and repel specks from it. He made the eyelashes black, so that their blackness would be a cause for gathering the light by which sight occurs, and a barrier against its dispersal, and it would be more eloquent in beauty and grace.

He, glorified is He, created twenty-four muscles for the movement of the pupil. If even one of them were lacking, the affair of the eye would be disrupted.

Since the eye resembles a mirror, which benefits only when it is at the utmost polish and clarity, He, glorified is He, made the eyelids move constantly to opening and closing, by the choice of the human and without his choice, so that the pupil remains pure and clear of all turbidities. He made the two eyes in the position of two polished mirrors in which the forms of external things are impressed. So the heart is affected, then what is in it appears upon them, and they are affected by it. Thus they are a mirror for what is in the heart, which appears in them, and a mirror for what is outside, whose form is imprinted in them. So the two eyes stand to the heart as the two glasses placed in a mirror. For this reason, the states of the eye are used as evidence for the states of the heart: its contentment and anger, its love and hatred, its aversion.

Among the most wondrous things is that the eye is among the most delicate of the body's organs, yet it is not affected by heat and cold as other dense organs are affected. Had the matter been merely a matter of nature, it would have been fitting for it to be the reverse, because the more delicate is quicker to be affected. So it is known that the attainment of these benefits is not merely by nature.

(Section)

Then turn to the two ears. Reflect on their split, their creation, and the placing of moisture in them so that they would aid in the perception of hearing. He made them two folds so that insects are prevented from entering the ear. He enclosed them with two shells (al-sadafatayn) that gather sound and convey it to the ear canal (al-simakh). He placed in the two shells convolutions so that the distance is lengthened, and the sharpness of the sound is broken, and insects do not enter at once, but their movements multiply, so that one notices them and expels them. He made the eyes in front and the ears behind, because the eyes are like the vanguard and the scout who goes before the people to reveal things to them, and like the lamp that lights for the traveller what is before him. As for the two ears, they perceive the absent meanings that come to the servant from in front of him, from behind him, and from his two sides. So placing them on the sides was the most just arrangement. Glory be to Him whose wisdom dazzles the intellects.

He made a covering for the eyes, because the perceiver of the ear is sounds, and sounds have no permanence. If a covering were placed over the ears, the sound would vanish before the covering was lifted, and the intended benefit would be lost. As for the perceiver of the eye, it is a fixed matter, and the eye needs a covering to protect it, and the presence of a covering does not affect perception.

Some of the scholars said: "The two eyes of a human are two guides, and his two ears are two messengers to his heart, and his tongue is an interpreter, and his two hands are two wings, and his two feet are two couriers, and the heart is the king. When the king is good, his armies are good, and when he is corrupt, his armies are corrupt."

(Section)

Then descend to the nose. Reflect on its form and its creation, and how He, glorified is He, raised it in the middle of the cheek in the most beautiful shape, and opened in it two passages, and placed in them the sense of smell, and made it an instrument for inhaling air and perceiving the various scents. Through the two nostrils one inhales cool and pleasant air, and thus one is spared from opening the mouth constantly. Had the two nostrils not existed, one would have needed an opening in the mouth at all times. He, glorified is He, made its cavity wide so that the air is confined within it and its coldness is broken before it reaches the brain. For the inhaled air divides into two portions: a portion, which is the greater part, passes to the lungs, and a portion passes to the brain. For this reason, cold air harms the one with a cold (al-mazkum) when he inhales it. He also placed in the nose an aid in articulating letters. He placed a partition between the two nostrils, and this is more eloquent in achieving the intended benefit, to the point that they are as two noses, like the two eyes, the two ears, the two hands, and the two feet. An affliction may strike one of the nostrils while the other remains sound. He made its cavity descend downward so that it would be the outlet for the waste that descends from the brain, and He covered it with a lasting covering so that those wastes do not appear in the sight of the beholder.

Consider the benefit of breath (al-nafas), which if cut off from a human he would perish. It is twenty-four thousand breaths in the day and night, the share of each hour being a thousand breaths.

Consider how the air enters the nostrils, where its coldness is broken, then it reaches the throat (al-halqum), where its temperament is balanced, then it reaches the lungs, where it is purified of its coarseness and turbidity, then it reaches the heart, purest and most balanced, so it refreshes it. Then it passes from it into the moving veins and advances to the farthest extremities of the body, then back to the lungs. Then, when it becomes very hot and exceeds the limit of benefit, it returns from those extremities to the body, then to the lungs, then to the throat, then to the nostrils, then it goes out and returns like it, and so forever. The totality of this is one breath. The Lord has counted the number of these breaths, and He has placed against each breath whatever ages He willed in Hellfire or in Paradise. How foolish is the one who wastes what is valued at this price for nothing.

(Section)

He, glorified is He, made the heart the commander of the body and the source of the innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizyah, the natural inborn heat). When the cool air is inhaled, it reaches the heart and its heat is balanced, and it remains there for a period. When it has become heated and burned, and it needs to be expelled and pushed out from it, the Most Wise of the wise did not waste that breath, nor bring it out without benefit. Rather, He made its expulsion a cause for the arising of sound. Then He placed in the larynx (al-hanjarah), the tongue and the palate, by their differing, sound, so that a letter (harf) comes into being. Then He inspired the human to combine that letter with its like and counterpart, so a word (kalimah) comes into being. Then He inspired him to combine that word with its like, so speech (kalam) comes into being.

So reflect on this dazzling wisdom: in bringing the breath to the heart to preserve its life, and then, when it is needed to be expelled and dispensed with, He made it a cause for this great benefit. Blessed is God, the best of creators.

He, glorified is He, created these passages and throats of differing shapes. Just as no two forms are alike, so no two sounds are alike in every respect. Rather, just as distinction between persons is attained through the faculty of sight, so it is attained through the faculty of hearing, so that distinction is attained by the blind and the seeing alike.

(Section)

Then descend to the chest, the mine of knowledge, forbearance, dignity, tranquillity, righteousness, and their opposites. You find the chests of the noble rising with righteousness, goodness, knowledge and benevolence, and the chests of the lowly seething with immorality, evils, wrongdoing, envy and deceit.

Then proceed from the courtyard of the chest to the observation of the heart, and you will find a great king seated upon the throne of his kingdom, commanding and forbidding, appointing and dismissing. Around him are gathered the princes, the ministers, and the soldiers, all in his service. If he is upright, they are upright; if he deviates, they deviate; if he is sound, they are sound; if he is corrupt, they are corrupt. Upon him rests the reliance, and he is the locus of the Lord's regard, the locus of His knowledge, love, fear, reliance upon Him, turning to Him, contentment with Him and from Him, and servitude to Him, first for himself and then, by extension, for his subjects and soldiers. So the most noble thing in the human is his heart. It is the one who knows God, strives toward Him, and loves Him. It is the locus of faith and gnosis (al-'irfan). It is the addressee to whom the messengers were sent, singled out with the noblest of gifts: faith and intellect. The limbs are only followers of the heart, which employs them as kings employ slaves and a shepherd his flock. What flows into the limbs of acts of obedience and disobedience are only its effects: if it becomes dark, the limbs darken, and if it is illuminated, they are illuminated. Yet despite this, it is between two fingers of the Most Merciful, mighty and majestic.

Glory be to the Turner of hearts, the Depositor of what He wills of the secrets of the unseen, who comes between a person and his heart, who knows what it contains of obedience to Him and of His religion, the Director of hearts as He wills and wherever He wills. He inspired the hearts of the saints, "Come to Me," so they hastened and stood before the Lord of the worlds. The Mighty and Majestic disliked the rising of others, so He held them back, and it was said, "Sit with those who sit."
