(Among the oaths most often sworn by the Messenger of God ﷺ was: "No, by the Turner of hearts.")

And among his supplications was: "O Turner of hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your obedience." Some of the early generation (al-salaf) said: "The heart is more subject to turning than a cooking pot when its boiling is at full force." Another said: "The heart is more subject to turning than a feather in a desert land on a day of violent wind."

The term "heart" (al-qalb) is applied to two meanings. The first is a sensible matter: the fleshy organ of conical shape (al-sanawbari), placed on the left side of the chest, within which is a cavity, and in the cavity is dark blood, and it is the source of the spirit (al-ruh). The second is a non-sensible matter: a divine, merciful, spiritual subtlety (lata'if rabbaniyyah rahmaniyyah ruhaniyyah) which has a connection and relation to this organ. That subtlety is the reality of the human.

The heart has two armies: an army seen by the eyes and an army seen by insight. As for its visible army, it is the outward and inward limbs, which have been created as servants to it, unable to oppose it. If it commands the eye to open, it opens; if it commands the tongue to speak, it speaks; if it commands the hand to strike, it strikes; if it commands the foot to walk, it walks. Likewise all the limbs, in submission to it.

When the heart was created for the journey to God and the Last Abode, and placed in this world to take provision from it, it needed a mount and provision for its journey for which it was created. So it was assisted by the limbs and faculties, which were subjected to it and set to its service, to bring to it what suits it of food and benefits, and to repel from it what harms and destroys it. So it needed an inner army, which is the will, the desire and the faculties, and an outer army, which is the limbs. He placed in the heart of wills and desires what it needs, and the limbs were created for it as the instruments of will. In repelling harms, it needs an inner army, which is anger that repels what destroys, and by which it takes vengeance upon enemies; and an outer army, which is the limbs through which its anger is executed, like weapons for fighting. This is not accomplished except by knowing what brings benefit and what repels harm. So the army of knowledge was added to it, which reveals to it the realities of what benefits it and what harms it.

When desire, anger and Satan were given power over it, it was assisted by an army of angels, and a permissible (halal) domain was made for it, in which to execute its desires, and opposite it were enemies upon whom its anger may be executed. Thus, whatever attribute it is tested with, He made for it an outlet and a locus through which to execute it. He made for the faculty of envy an outlet, namely rivalry in doing good, longing for it, and racing to it. For the faculty of pride He made an outlet, namely pride against the enemies of God, the Exalted, and humiliating them. The Prophet ﷺ said to one he saw strutting between the two lines in battle: "Indeed, it is a gait that God dislikes except in this place." And God, glorified is He, has commanded harshness toward His enemies.

For the faculty of greed He made an outlet: greed for what benefits, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Be eager for what benefits you." For the faculty of desire He made an outlet: marriage with up to four wives and taking concubines as one wills. For the faculty of love of wealth He made an outlet: spending it in pursuit of God's pleasure and taking provision from it for the Hereafter. So love of wealth in this manner is not blameworthy. For the love of rank and standing He made an outlet: employing it to execute His commands, establish His religion, support the oppressed, relieve the distressed, aid the weak, and suppress the enemies of God. So love of leadership and standing in this manner is worship. For the faculty of play and amusement He made an outlet: play with one's wife, or with his bow and arrow, or training his horse, and everything that aids the truth. For the faculty of cunning and deceit He made an outlet: outwitting his enemy and the enemy of God by various kinds of stratagem, until he humbles him and returns him disgraced, and using against him the kinds of deceit that his enemy uses against him. Thus for all the faculties that were fixed in him He made an outlet for each, and God fixed them in him for benefits which His wisdom required. He does not seek their suspension. Rather, their channels are redirected from one place to another and from one locus to another. Whoever reflects on this locus and comprehends it knows the intensity of need for it and the greatness of benefit from it.

(Section)

The totality of the paths and doors by which the heart and its armies are guarded is four. Whoever controls them, balances them, sets their channels right, and directs them to their fitting places benefits thereby, his heart and limbs benefit, and his enemy does not gloat over him. They are: greed, desire, anger and envy. These four are the principal junctions of the paths of evil and good. Just as they are paths to eternal punishment, they are paths to everlasting bliss. Adam, father of humankind, was expelled from the Garden through greed, then he was readmitted to it through greed, but there is a difference between his first greed and his second greed. The father of the jinn was expelled from it through envy, and then he was not granted a rivalry and envy that would return him to it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom God has given wealth and empowered him to spend it in the right way, and a man whom God has given the Qur'an and who stands with it through the hours of the night and the ends of the day."

As for anger, it is the ghoul of the intellect, which ravages it as the wolf ravages the sheep. The greatest thing that Satan preys upon is one's anger and desire. When his greed is only for what benefits him, and his envy is rivalry in good, and his anger is for God against His enemies, and his desire is employed in what is permitted to him and aids him in what he is commanded, these four do not harm him; rather, he benefits from them to the greatest degree.

(Section)

When you reflect on the state of the heart between the angel and Satan, you will see the most wondrous of wonders. This one visits it at one time, and that one visits it at another. When the angel visits it, there arises from his visitation expansion, openness, light, mercy, sincerity, turning to God, love of God and preferring Him over all else, shortening of hope, withdrawal from the abode of trial, test and delusion. If that state persisted for it, it would be in the most pleasant, sweetest and purest of lives. But the visitation of Satan comes to it and produces constriction, darkness, anxiety, grief, fear, displeasure at what is decreed, doubt about the truth, greed for this world and its immediate gains, and heedlessness of God, which is among the greatest torments of the heart.

Then, people in this trial are of varying ranks, which none can count but God. Some have the visitation of the angel more dominant and stronger than the visitation of Satan. When Satan visits such a one, he finds pain, constriction, confinement and bad condition in proportion to the life of the heart that he has. So he hastens to drive away that visitation and does not let it become firmly established, lest it become difficult to remedy. He is always in a war between the two visitations: sometimes one prevails over him and sometimes he prevails over it, and the final outcome is for piety.

Others have the visitation of Satan more dominant and stronger over them. The visitation of the angel keeps being overcome until it becomes firmly established and the ruling is for it, and the heart dies and does not perceive what Satan has inflicted on it, even though it is in utmost torment, constriction and confinement. But the intoxication of desire and heedlessness veils from it the perception of that pain. When the veil is lifted, it is possible for it to remedy it with the medicine and eradicate it. But if the veil returns, the matter returns as it was, until the time of departure from this world uncovers it. Then those pains, cares, griefs and sorrows appear, though they were not newly renewed for it, but were latent, concealed by preoccupations. When the preoccupations are removed, what was latent appears, and its like multiplied renews itself for it.

(Section)

Satan visits the heart because there are attractions there that draw him. These are of two kinds: attributes and volitions. When the attractions are attributes, his authority becomes strong there, his affair grows powerful, and he finds a footing and a settled abode. Then remembrances, supplications and seeking refuge come like the speech of the soul and do not repel Satan's authority, because his vehicle is a constant attribute. But when the servant uproots those attributes and works to purify himself of them and cleanse himself, Satan remains in the heart only as passing thoughts, whisperings and visitations without settling. This weakens him and strengthens the visitation of the angel, so remembrances, supplications and seeking refuge come and repel him with the easiest thing.

If you want a precise example for this, its likeness is that of a dog extremely hungry, and between you and it is meat or bread. It is watching you and seeing you, unable to contend with you, though it is closer than you. You rebuke it and shout at it, but it refuses except to attack you and plunder what is before you. The remembrances are like shouting at it and rebuking it. But its object and its aim are before you, and you have drawn it near you. When nothing before you suits it, and it has observed you and seen that you are stronger than it, you rebuke it and shout at it, and it goes away. Likewise the heart empty of Satan's power is restrained by mere remembrance.

As for the heart in which those attributes exist, which are its mount and abode, remembrance falls on its edges and sides, and it is not able to expel the enemy from it. The evidence for this you will find in prayer. So reflect on your state and see whether the prayer, with its remembrances and recitation, expels Satan from your heart and empties it entirely for God, the Exalted, and sets it before its Lord, turning to Him with all of itself, praying to God as if seeing Him, with all its concern gathered upon God and its remembrance, its watchfulness, its love and its intimacy with Him in the place of thoughts and whisperings, or not. And God is the One sought for help.

And here is a point that must be grasped: hearts filled with corrupt humours are treated by acts of worship, remembrance and seeking refuge, which are medicines for those humours, just as medicine stirs up the humours of the body. If there is no dietary regimen (hamiyah) before and after the medicine, the medicine only stirs them further. If it removes something of them, the matter depends on two things: the regimen and the use of the medicines.

(Section)

The first thing that knocks on the heart is a passing thought (khatrah). If one repels it, one is at rest from what follows. If one does not repel it, it grows stronger and becomes a whispered suggestion (waswasah), and repelling it then becomes harder. If one hastens and repels it, well and good; otherwise it grows stronger and becomes a desire (shahwah). If one treats it, well and good; otherwise it becomes a resolve (iradah). If one treats it, well and good; otherwise it becomes a determination (azimah). Once it reaches this state, it cannot be repelled, the deed becomes attached to it without fail, and what one could once do by a mere first step is no longer possible. At that point the treatment passes to the strongest remedy, which is complete purging through sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh).

There is no doubt that repelling the beginnings of this disease from the outset is easier and lighter than purging it after it has taken hold, if fate assists and success is granted. Repelling is the better course for it. If the soul is pained by parting from a beloved thing, let it weigh the loss of this lowly beloved, whose pleasure is cut off and mixed with pains and worries, against the loss of the supreme beloved, which is lasting, and to which this beloved bears no comparison at all, neither in its worth nor in its duration. Let it weigh the pain of losing the one against the pain of losing the lowly beloved. Let it weigh the pleasure of turning in repentance (inabah) and facing toward God Most High, and delighting in His love, His remembrance and His obedience, against the pleasure of turning toward base vices and committing ugly acts. Let it weigh the pleasure of gaining a sin against the pleasure of gaining over an enemy, and the pleasure of sin against the pleasure of chastity (iffah); the pleasure of sin against the pleasure of strength and of subduing the enemy; the pleasure of sin against the pleasure of humbling his enemy and turning him back abased and humiliated; the pleasure of sin against the pleasure of obedience, which stands between him and his desire; and the loss of his desire against the loss of God Most High's praise and that of His angels upon him, the loss of His fine recompense and abundant reward. Let it weigh the joy of attaining it against the joy of leaving it for God Most High's sake, both in this world and in the next, and in the joy of what He will praise him for in his worldly life and in the Hereafter. And God is the One sought for help.

This is a section that the discourse led to through God Most High's words: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾

We have alluded to it briefly; had we pursued it fully, it would have required many volumes. Yet what we have mentioned serves as a reminder of what we have left out. And success is from God.

(Section)

He said in (Shifa' al-'Alil):

When you contemplate the organs present in a person, and contemplate their functions and benefits, and the wisdom each one contains that is specific to it, such as its shape, its attributes, its temperament, and its placement in the person in that specific position, you will know with certainty that all of this proceeds from one Creator, one Director and one Wise One.

Then move from this to the individuals of the world, one by one, of the human kind, and you will find the single wisdom manifest in these many individuals benefiting one another and aiding one another: the ploughman for the sower, the sower for the reaper, the weaver for the tailor, the tailor for the carpenter, and the carpenter for the builder. This one helps that one with his hand, that one with his foot, another helps him with his eye, another with his ear, another with his tongue, and another with his wealth.

Since none of them can secure all his own interests or fulfil all his needs, and since no single one of them possesses all the properties of his kind, they, with their many individuals, are like one human being, each part attending to the interests of the others. The properties of humanity are perfected in their attributes, actions, crafts and what is required of them. For the individual cannot combine all the scholarly and practical virtues, strength and endurance. So this was placed in the human species as a whole. God, glorified is He, has dispersed the perfections of the species among its individuals, and has given each individual that for which he is prepared and receptive, such that if more were said, He would give it, for He is generous in His essence. His generosity and goodness overflow upon the whole world, and His bounty exceeds by manifold what has overflowed upon it. He bestows it continually across the successive moments, forever.

Likewise, He bestows bounty in Paradise, and His bounty remains over and above its people. He creates for it a creation to inhabit its abundance. The specification of His bounty corresponds to the preparedness of the agents and preparatory causes, and that is by His will and wisdom. He is the One who brought them into being, the One who prepared them, and the One who sustains them.

Since His generosity and bounty are broader than the needs of creation, it was necessary that much of it should remain spread through existence, unused and neglected. This is like the light of the sun, for example: the welfare of animals is not complete without it, yet it shines upon places that exceed the needs of the children of Adam and of animals. Likewise the rain, the plants, and all other blessings. Yet their existence is not rendered void of wisdom, benefits, lessons and indications. The gift and blessings of the Lord are broader than the needs of His creatures, so there must remain in the waters, the sustenance, the plants and other things some neglected portions.

And it should not be said: "What is the wisdom in creating them?"

For this is the question of an ignorant and wrongdoing person. The wisdom in creating the earth and what is upon it is manifest to every discerning eye, though only part of it is inhabited, not all of it. The Lord, exalted is He, is vast in generosity and everlasting in it, so His generosity and goodness are general and enduring, and cannot be otherwise, for that is a necessity of His knowledge, power and wisdom. To His knowledge, power and wisdom belong generality, comprehensiveness and absolute perfection in every respect. From a survey of the world and its conditions one knows that it ends in one Knowing One, one Powerful One and one Wise One, who perfected its order in the best perfection and brought it into being in the most complete existence. He, glorified is He, arranges the actions of the agents despite their multiplicity, binds some of them to others, helps some of them through others, makes some of them a cause for others and an end for others. This is among the strongest proofs that He is one Creator, one Lord and one Powerful One. The multiplicity and variety of His actions at a single time, and their succession across successive moments, indicate His power. The determination of His dispositions over His creatures despite their number indicates it. His knowledge and wisdom are indicated by the fact that everything, great and small, subtle and sublime, enters into the wise order, and nothing is outside it, not even the pores of hair in the skin, the glands of saliva in the mouth, or the fine channels of the veins in the smallest animals that our eyes cannot perceive and our power cannot reach. This holds for what is subtle in its smallness and for what is vast in its greatness, such as the winds that carry the clouds to the barren earth where there is no plant, and rain them down upon it, so that by it there comes forth vegetation, by it animals are given life, and in it He places two portions of food, drink, sustenance and medicines. Leave aside what lies beyond this: the subjection of the sun, the moon and the stars, and the variation of their risings and settings to establish the reign of night and day and the seasons of the year, by which the order of the welfare of those upon the earth is maintained.

When you contemplate the world, you find it like a built house, prepared, in which all His servants dwell: the sky is its roof, the earth its carpet, the stars its adornment, the sun its lamp and the means of its inhabitants' welfare. The night is their resting place, the day their livelihood, the rain their watering, the plants their nourishment, their cure and their fruit, and the animals their servants, from which they gain food and clothing. The jewels are their treasures and stores. Each thing among them is for what suits it. The kinds of plants serve all their needs, and the varieties of animals are prepared for all their welfare. That is the strongest proof of the oneness of its Creator and His power.

(Section)

Renew your reflection on yourself, and on the wisdom of the All-Knowing Creator in your creation. Look at the senses through which you overlook things, how God placed them in the head like lamps atop a minaret, so that you may be able to observe things through them. He did not place them in the limbs that are subjected to degradation, like the two hands and the two feet, which would be exposed to afflictions through the handling of tasks and movements. Nor did He place them in the organs in the middle of the body, like the belly and the back, for then turning and looking at things would be difficult for you. Since none of these organs had a place for them, the head was the most fitting and most beautiful place for them. The head is the watchtower of the senses. Then reflect on the wisdom in His making the senses five, corresponding to the five sensible objects, so that each is met by its counterpart, lest any sensible object be left without a sense that can perceive it. He made sight corresponding to visible things, hearing corresponding to sounds, smell corresponding to the various kinds of odours, taste corresponding to flavours that are tasted, and touch corresponding to tangible things. So what sensible object remains without a sense? Had there been among sensible objects anything other than these, He would have given you a sixth sense for it. And since whatever lies beyond these is perceived by the inner faculty, He gave you the inner senses, namely these fives about which the common and special custom has run, where they say of the thinker who ponders: "He multiplied his fives by his sixes," meaning that his fives are his five senses and his sixes are his six directions. They intended by this that the heart draws him and carries him through the regions and directions, so that from the intensity of his thought he turns his five senses over in his six directions and multiplies them there.

(Section)

Then these senses were aided by other created things external to them, which serve as intermediaries in their perception. Sight was aided by light and radiance; without them the viewer would benefit nothing from his eye, and if light and radiance were withheld, the eye would profit nothing. Hearing was aided by air, which carries sounds through the atmosphere and then delivers them to the ear, which receives them and then transmits them to the faculty of hearing. Without air a man would hear nothing. Smell was aided by the gentle breeze, which carries the scent and then conveys it to the organ so that it perceives it; without it, it would smell nothing. Taste was aided by the saliva dissolved in the mouth, through which the faculty of taste perceives the flavours of things. For this reason saliva itself has no flavour, neither sweet, nor sour, nor salty, nor pungent, because it would transform those flavours into its own taste, and its purpose would not be achieved. Touch was aided by a power God placed within it, by which it perceives tangible things, and it did not need anything from outside, unlike the other senses. It perceives tangible things without any intermediary between them, because it perceives them by contact and touching, and so it needs no intermediary.

(Section)

Then reflect on the condition of one who lacks sight, and the defects that befall his affairs. He does not know where his foot is placed, does not see what is before him, does not distinguish colours or beautiful sights from ugly ones, and cannot gain knowledge from a book he reads, nor is he able to take lessons from or contemplate the wonders of God's kingdom. Moreover, he is unaware of many of his benefits and harms: he does not perceive a pit into which he is about to fall, nor an animal such as a predator that targets him, so he cannot guard against it, nor an enemy rushing at him to kill him, nor can he escape if he is sought. Rather he is open to whoever intends harm to him. Were it not for God's special protection of him, close to the protection of a child and His guardianship, his destruction would be likelier than his safety. He is like meat on a chopping block. For this reason God made his reward, if he is patient and seeks it, Paradise. And among the perfection of His kindness is that He turned the light of his sight into his insight, so that he is the most perceptive of people and the most intuitive. He gathers his concern upon Him, so his heart is united upon Him and not scattered, that life may be pleasant for him and his welfare complete, and one should not think he is sorrowful, grieving or regretful. This is the judgement on one born blind.

As for one who lost his eyesight after having sight, he is in the position of all the other people of affliction who pass from well-being to calamity. The trial is severe for him, because he has been cut off from what he was accustomed to of sights and forms and from the benefits of his sight. So his case has another judgement. Likewise one who lacks hearing: he loses the spirit of address and conversation, is deprived of the delight of discourse and the melody of sweet voices, and people find it burdensome to address him, and grow weary of him. He hears nothing of people's reports and talk. Among them he is a present one who is like an absent one, a living one who is like a dead one, and a near one who is like a distant one. The theologians (nuzzar) have disputed which of the two is closer to perfection and less disabled in his affairs: the blind man or the deaf man. They have mentioned various considerations for this. This rests on another principle, namely which of the two qualities is more perfect: the quality of hearing or the quality of sight. We have mentioned the dispute over both earlier in this book, and we mentioned people's views and their proofs, and the verification of the matter.

Whichever of the two qualities is more perfect, the harm of lacking it is greater. What is appropriate in this place is to say: the one lacking sight is more harmed of the two, sounder in religion, and better in outcome, while the one lacking hearing is less harmed in his worldly life, more ignorant in his religion, and worse in outcome. For when one lacks hearing, he lacks admonitions and counsels, the doors of beneficial knowledge are closed to him, and the paths of desires, which sight perceives, open before him, and he gains no knowledge that restrains him from them. So his harm in religion is greater, and the blind man's harm in worldly life is greater. For this reason there was no deaf man among the Companions, while there were a number of blind men among them. And it is rare that God tests His friends with deafness, while He tests many of them with blindness.

This is the decisive word on this question: the harm of deafness lies in religion, the harm of blindness lies in this world, and the one healthy is the one whom God has granted health from both, and has provided him with his hearing and sight, and made them his heirs.

(Section)

As for one who lacks the two forms of explanation, the explanation of the heart and the explanation of the tongue, he is in the position of the dumb animals, and indeed his condition is better than theirs. For they have what they were created for, the benefits and interests for which they are used, whereas he is ignorant of much of what the animals are guided to, and casts himself into what the animals restrain themselves from. The lack of the explanation of the tongue, while the explanation of the heart is intact, is less severe than the lack of the explanation of the heart. And for one who lacks the distinctive feature of the human being, which is speech, the burden is intensified and his grief is great, and he lingers long in regret for being unable to answer and to return a reply. He is like a paralysed person who sees what he needs but his hand and foot cannot reach it. How many abundant blessings God has bestowed upon His servant in these organs, limbs, faculties and benefits within him, yet he pays them no attention and does not thank God for them. Were he to lose any one of them, he would wish that he possessed it even if he had the world and all that is in it. He turns about in God's blessings through the soundness of his organs, limbs and faculties, yet he is bare of gratitude for them. If the world with all that is in it were offered to him in exchange for the loss of one of them, he would refuse the exchange, knowing that it would be a bad bargain. Indeed, man is truly a wrongdoer, ungrateful.

(Section)

Then reflect on His wisdom in the organs created in you singly, in pairs, in threes and in fours, and the profound wisdoms in that. The head, the tongue, the nose and the male organ were each created singly only, since there is no benefit in their being more than that. Do you not see that if another head were added to the head, the body would be burdened without need for it, because all the senses that are needed are gathered in one head. Further, if the human being were divided by his head into two parts, and he spoke with one and heard with it, saw with it, smelled with it and tasted with it, the other would remain idle with no purpose in it. If he spoke, saw and heard with both together, a single speech, a single hearing and a single sight, the other would be superfluous with no benefit in it. If their perceptions differed, his conditions and perceptions would differ with them. Likewise, if he had two tongues in one mouth, then if he spoke with both a single speech, one of them would be wasted; if he spoke with one without the other, it is the same; and if he spoke with both at once in two different speeches, he would confuse the listener, who would not know which of the two speeches to take. Likewise, if he had two heads and two mouths, then, along with the ugliness of his form, one of them would be superfluous with no benefit in it. This is in contrast to the organs created in pairs, such as the two eyes, the two ears, the two lips, the two hands, the two feet, the two shins, the two thighs, the two hips and the two breasts, for the wisdom in them is evident, their interest is manifest, and beauty and adornment are apparent in them. Had the human being had only one eye, he would have been of a disfigured and deficient form. The same applies to the two eyebrows.

And as for the two hands, the two legs, the two shins and the two thighs, their being in pairs is essential for the human being, and his welfare is not complete without it. Do you not see how a person who has lost one of his hands or one of his legs is left in a state of helplessness and incapacity? If the carpenter, the tailor, the blacksmith, the baker, the builder and the other craftsmen, whose crafts cannot be carried out except with two hands, had one of their hands paralysed, their craft would be rendered useless to them. Therefore wisdom required that of this kind of limbs and members He give two, two. Likewise He gave two lips, because his welfare is not complete without them. In them are many kinds of benefit: speech, taste, covering the mouth, beauty, adornment, kissing, and other things.

As for the three-part members, they are the sides of the nose and its walls, and we have already mentioned the wisdom in this earlier. As for the four-part members, they are the four ankle bones, which are the meeting point of the two feet and that which holds them together; by them the strength and movement of the two feet exist, and in them are the benefits of the two shins. Likewise the eyelids of the two eyes contain wisdom and benefits: they are a covering for the eyes, a protection for them, a beauty and an adornment, and other wisdoms. So the perfect wisdom required that the limbs be made as they are in number, shape and form. If they were to increase or decrease, that would be a deficiency in the creation. For this reason there are found in the human species those who are extra in creation and those who are lacking in it, which points to the wisdom of the Lord, exalted is He. {And if He had willed, He would have made all His creatures thus.} And so that the one who is perfect in creation knows the completeness of the blessing upon him, and that He created him as a well-formed, balanced creature, not adding to his creation what he has no need of, nor diminishing from it what he needs, as he sees in others. Thus he is more worthy of increasing in gratitude and praise to his Lord, and he knows that this is not the work of nature, but the work of God who perfected everything He created, and who creates what He wills.

(Section)

From where does nature obtain this variation and difference which exists in the human species among their forms? It is rare to see two people who are alike in every respect, and this is among the rarest things in the world, unlike the kinds of animals, such as cattle, wild beasts, birds and all other creatures. For you see a herd of gazelles, a flock of sheep, a group of camels, or a drove of cattle, resembling one another so much that one cannot distinguish one of them from another except after long reflection or by a clear sign. But people differ in their forms and creation, so that hardly two of them come together in one attribute and one creation; rather, not even one voice and one throat. The profound wisdom in this is that people need to recognise one another by their eyes and their features, because of the dealings that take place among them. Had it not been for the difference and variation in forms, their conditions would have been corrupted and their order scattered; the witness would not be known from the one testified against, nor the debtor from the creditor, nor the seller from the buyer. A man would not know his wife from another woman because of the mixing, nor would she know her husband from another. In that would be the greatest corruption and disorder. Who, then, distinguished between their features, forms and voices, and set between them differences that speech cannot reach and description cannot grasp? Ask the one who denies the Creator: is this the act of nature?

And is there in nature a requirement for this variation and differentiation within the species? Where is the claim of the naturalists that its action is uniform, because it is one in itself, does not act by will or intention, so that the variation of its actions is impossible? How then can the denier of the Creator combine this with that?

{For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but the hearts which are in the breasts are blinded.} [Qur'an 22:46]

It sometimes happens within the human species that two people resemble each other so closely that one can hardly tell them apart, so the burden in dealing with them becomes great, and there is a strong need to distinguish the one who deserves from the one held to account for his sin, and the one who owes the right.

If this occurs frequently in resemblance of names, and the witness and the judge meet with what they meet of that, what then would one think if resemblance were placed in creation and form? And since beasts, birds and wild animals are not harmed in the least by this resemblance, wisdom did not call for distinguishing between every pair of them. Blessed is God, the best of creators, whose wisdom encompasses everything.

(Section)

Then reflect on why, when man and woman reach maturity, they both share in the growth of pubic hair, and then the man is distinguished from the woman by the beard. For when Almighty God made the man a guardian over the woman, and made her like a servant to him, and the captive in his hands, He distinguished him over her by what gives him humility, honour, dignity and majesty, because of his perfection and his need for that. And He prevented the woman from having it, for the full enjoyment of her and the pleasure of her, so that the freshness and beauty of her face would remain, which hair would not spoil; and they share in the rest of the hair for the wisdom and benefit in it.

(Section)

Then reflect on this sound that comes out of the throat, and the preparation of its instruments, and speech and its arrangement, and the letters and their points of articulation, their tools, their syllables and their resonances. You will find remarkable wisdom in a simple air that comes out from the chest, travels through the tube of the windpipe until it reaches the throat, the tongue, the lips and the teeth, and there it produces at each point of articulation and each end a clear resonance, separate from the other, by which a letter arises. It is one simple sound running through one channel until it reaches points and limits, from which twenty-nine letters are heard, on which all speech revolves: its command, its prohibition, its information, its questioning, its verse, its prose, its sermons, its exhortations and its superfluities. Among it is that which makes one laugh, and that which makes one weep; that which causes despair, and that which gives hope; that which frightens, and that which brings hope and consolation; that which saddens, that which restrains the soul and the limbs, and that which energises them; that which makes the healthy ill and heals the sick. Among it is that which removes blessings and brings down punishments, and that by which calamity is averted and favours are drawn down, by which hearts are won over, by which those who hate one another are joined, and by which enemies are made allies; and among it is what is the opposite of these. Among it is the word which its speaker does not heed, by which he falls into the Fire, further than the distance between East and West; and the word which its speaker does not heed, by which he is raised to the highest heights of Paradise in the presence of the Lord of the worlds.

Glory be to Him who produced all of that from a simple air that comes out of the chest, which one does not know for what it is intended, nor where it ends, nor where its resting place is. Add to this the variety of tongues and languages, which none can count but God. A crowd of people gathers from different lands, and each speaks in his own language, so that different languages are heard as one coherent, ordered speech, and each does not understand what the other is saying. Yet the tongue, which is one organ, is the same in shape and appearance; likewise the throat, the molars, the lips, and yet speech varies with the greatest variation. The sign in this is like the sign in the earth, which is watered with one water, yet there come out of it, along with that, kinds of plants, flowers, grains and fruits: these varied and differing kinds. For this reason God, glorified is He, informed in His Book that in each of these there are signs, so He said: {And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your tongues and your colours. Indeed in that are signs for those who know.} [Qur'an 30:22]

And He said: {And on the earth are adjacent tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees, some with multiple trunks and some with single trunks, watered with one water.} [Qur'an 13:4] and the rest of the verse.

Now look at the throat, how it is like a tube for the sound to come out, and the tongue, the lips and the teeth for shaping the letters and tones. Do you not see that the one whose teeth have fallen out cannot produce the letters that come out of them and from the tongue? And the one whose lip has been lost, how can he not produce the letters ra and lam? And the one who has an affliction in his throat, how can he not manage the throat letters? Anatomists have likened the exit of the sound to the reed-pipe, and the lung to the bellows which one blows into from below so that air enters it, and the membranes which squeeze the lung so that the sound comes out of the throat, to the hands that squeeze the bellows until the air comes out through the reed; and the lips and teeth which shape the sound into letters and tones, to the fingers that move over the pipe and shape it into melodies, and the tonal points at which the sound ends, to the holes in the reed. So much so that it has been said that the pipe was made in the image of this in man. So if you marvel at the craft which human hands produce until these sounds come out of it, then how much more should you marvel at the divine craft which brought forth those letters and sounds from flesh, blood, veins and bones! How great is the distance between them! But what is familiar and customary does not strike the souls with wonder. When they see something that has no comparison to it at all, except that it is strange to them, they receive it with wonder and with glorification of the Lord, exalted is He. And with them are His marvellous and dazzling signs which are greater than that, which analogy cannot grasp. Then reflect on the variation of these tones and the difference of these sounds, despite the similarity of the throats, the windpipes, the tongues, the lips and the teeth. Who, other than the All-Creating, the All-Knowing, distinguished between them with the most complete distinction, despite the similarity of their places?

(Section)

In these instruments there are other purposes and benefits apart from the benefit of speech. In the throat is the passage of the cool breeze which refreshes the heart with this constant, continuous breath. In the tongue is the benefit of taste: by it flavours are tasted, their pleasure is perceived, and by it one distinguishes between them, so that the reality of each is known. In addition, the tongue helps in swallowing food, and in turning it and rolling it until its passage through the throat becomes easy. In the teeth are benefits that are known from cutting food, as has been mentioned. In them is the support of the lips and holding them back from drooping and disfiguring the face; for this reason you see that the one whose teeth have fallen out has lips that droop. In the lips are many benefits: by them one sips drinks, so that what enters the throat is in measured quantity, and the drinker does not choke on it. Then they are a closed door over the mouth, where what comes out of the inner body ends, and from which what enters begins. They are a covering and a lid over it: the gatekeeper opens them whenever he wishes and closes them whenever he wishes. They are also a beauty and an adornment for the face, and in them are other benefits besides that. Look at the one whose lips have fallen off, how ugly his appearance is. It has become clear that each of these organs is used for many kinds of benefit, purposes and interests, just as one tool is used for various works.

Moreover, if you were to see the brain and it were uncovered for you about its composition and structure, you would see wonders, and there would be revealed to you a composition in which the intellect is bewildered, wrapped in veils, and covered with membranes, some above others, to protect it from harm and preserve it from disturbance. Then the skull closes over it like a helmet and an iron shield, so that it protects the brain from the blow, the fall and the strike that reach it, which the shield receives on its behalf, like the helmet on the head of a warrior. Then that skull is covered with the skin of the scalp, which shields the bone from being exposed to harm. Then that scalp is clothed in a robe of abundant hair, as a protection for it, a shelter against heat, cold and harm, and as a beauty and an adornment for it. Ask the one who denies the Creator: who fortified the brain with this fortification, and measured it with this measure, and made it a treasury in which He deposited such benefits, powers and wonders as He deposited? Then He sealed that treasury firmly and fortified it with the most complete fortification, and guarded it with the greatest protection, and made it the source of the senses and perceptions. And who placed the eyelids over the two eyes like a covering, and the eyelashes like bolts, and the eyebrows like shelves above them when they are open? And who assembled its various layers, one layer above another, until they reached the number of the seven heavens, and made for each layer a benefit and use, so that if one layer were disordered, the sight would be disordered? And who split them in the face in the finest split, and gave them the finest shape, and placed beauty in them, and made them a mirror of the heart, a lookout, a guardian of the body, and a scout whom it sends out like soldiers on their missions, who do not tire or grow weary despite their frequent travel and long journeys? And who placed the seeing light in them in the size of the lens of the eye, so that in it one sees the heavens and the earth, the mountains, the sun, the moon, the seas and the wonders from within seven layers? And who placed them on the highest part of the face like a sentry on a lofty hill, a guardian for the body? And who veiled the King in the breasts, and seated him there upon the throne of the kingdom, and set the armies of the limbs, the inner and outer powers, to serve him, and made them subservient to him? So they obey him when he commands them, they desist when he forbids them, they listen to him, obey him, toil and strive to please him, and they cannot escape from him nor leave his command. Among them is his messenger, among them his courier, among them his interpreter, among them his helpers, and each of them works at a task it does not go beyond, and does not act in any other task. Then, when he wishes rest, he commands them to be still and quiet so that the king may take his rest. When he awakes from his sleep, his soldiers stand before him at their tasks and go wherever they are directed, persistent and never slackening. If you were to witness him in the place of his kingdom, with the affairs and decrees issuing from him and coming to him, the armies in his service, and messengers passing between him and his army and his subjects, you would see for him a wondrous state. So what has the ignorant and heedless person missed of the wonders, lessons and insights which need no long journeys or crossing of deserts? God, the Exalted, said: {And on the earth are signs for those who are certain, and in yourselves. Will you not then see?} [Qur'an 51:20-21] So He called His servants to reflect upon themselves, and to infer from them the Originator and Fashioner. Had it not been for this, we would not have expanded the discussion on this subject, nor extended ourselves to this extent. But the lesson in it is evident, the benefit is great, and reflection upon it is among the things that increase the believer's faith. How many guards are there beneath the heart, how many servants does it have, how many slaves, yet it is unaware of them! Whatever God created for it, prepared for it, desired from it, and prepared for it of honour and bliss or humiliation and punishment: whether it sits on the throne of the kingdom in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign Almighty, looking upon the face of his Lord and hearing His address; or whether it is a prisoner in the greatest prison, amid layers of fire, in painful torment. If this king understood what was prepared for him, he would hold back his kingdom and strive for the kingdom that does not end and does not perish. But veils of heedlessness have been drawn over him: {That God might accomplish a matter which was destined to be done.} [Qur'an 8:42]

(Section)

And whoever placed in the throat two openings, one for the sound and one for the breath reaching the lung.

And the other is for food and drink, which is the gullet (al-mari'), reaching the stomach. He placed between them a barrier that prevents either from passing along the other's path. Had food entered through the opening of breath into the lungs, it would have destroyed the living creature. And He made the lungs a fan for the heart, cooling it constantly, never ceasing or slackening, so that the heat would not be confined within it and perish. He made openings for the waste products of nourishment and made for them sphincters (ishrajat) that hold them back, so that they would not flow continuously and spoil a person's life and keep people from sitting with one another. He made the stomach as firm as the strongest sinew, because it was prepared for cooking and ripening food. Were it soft flesh, it would itself be cooked and ripened, so He made it like a tough sinew, to be strong enough for cooking and ripening, and so that the fire beneath it would not wear it out. He made the liver thin and smooth, because it was prepared to receive the pure, fine part of nourishment and to digest it, and its work is finer than the work of the stomach. He protected the delicate, thin brain within hard bone tubes, to keep it and guard it, so that it does not decay or melt. He made the flowing blood held and confined within the veins, like water in a vessel, so that it is controlled and does not run loose. He made the nails on the tips of the fingers as a shield and protection for them against work and crafts. He made the inside of the ear smooth, shaped like a star (kawkab), so that sound would spread within it until it reaches the inner hearing, and the sharpness of the air has been broken, so it does not strike it harshly, and so that air finds it difficult to penetrate before it is held back, and so that it holds whatever dust and filth might settle in it. And there are other wisdoms besides these. He made more flesh on the thighs and hips than on the rest of the limbs, to protect them from the ground, so that their bones do not ache from prolonged sitting, as ache the bones of one whose body has wasted and whose flesh has diminished from long sitting, where nothing stands between him and the ground. He made the water of the eyes salty, to protect them from melting; the water of the ear bitter, to protect it from flies, air and mosquitoes; and the water of the mouth sweet, by which one perceives the tastes of things, so that no other taste mixes with them. He placed the door of excretion in the human being in the most concealed place, just as a wise architect places the latrine in the most hidden place in the house.

Likewise the outlet of excretion in the human being is in the most concealed place. It does not protrude behind, nor rise up in front, but is hidden in an obscure part of the body, where the two thighs meet, with what flesh is on them, concealed. When the time of need comes and a person sits for it, that outlet opens to the earth.

He made the teeth sharp for cutting food and dividing it, and the molars broad for crushing and grinding it. He stripped the nails of the human being of sensation and feeling, because they grow long and extend, and there is need to take them and trim them. Had He given them sensation, they would have hurt him, and it would have been difficult for him to cut whatever he wished from them. And if they felt, a person would have fallen into one of two calamities: either leaving them until they grew long, became unsightly and burdensome to him, or enduring the pain of cutting them.

As for the pain and ache of cutting them, and He made the palm's inner surface unable to grow hair, because if it had hair, touch would be impaired for a person, and many of the works done by the hand would be hard for him. For this same wisdom, the chest of the man was not made able to grow hair, since hair there would prevent intercourse. And since the matter (of the body) required hair to grow there, hair grew around the genitals of man and woman. For this same wisdom, hair was stripped from the lips and likewise the inside of the mouth, and likewise the sole of the foot, its underside and upper side, because they meet dust, filth, mud and thorns. Had there been hair there, it would have harmed a person greatly and he would carry from the ground at all times what would burden him. This is not only for the human being: you see that the beasts are all covered with hair, while these places are left bare of it for this wisdom. Do you not see how the divine craftsmanship removed the aspects of error and harm and brought all that is correct, beneficial and in the interest of the creature?

When those who attack wisdom and find fault with creation sought faults in what they criticize, they faulted the hair under the armpits, the pubic hair, the hair inside the nose, and the hair of the knees, and they said: "What wisdom is in it, and what benefit?" This comes from the excess of their ignorance and the feebleness of their minds. Wisdom need not be entirely known to mankind, nor most of it. Indeed, what they know has no proportion to what they do not know of it. Were the knowledge of all creatures measured against the aspects of God's wisdom in His creation and command, and against what is hidden from them, it would be like a sparrow's peck in the sea. It is enough for the discerning intelligent person to infer from what is known of it what is not known, and to know that the wisdom in what he does not know is like its wisdom in what he knows, rather, greater and more subtle.

The likeness of these fools and dullards is only that of a man with no knowledge of the subtleties of crafts and sciences such as building, engineering, medicine, even weaving, sewing and carpentry. When he sets out to object with his corrupt intellect against their masters regarding some of their tools, their crafts and the arrangement of their work, and it is hidden from him, he declares everything hidden from him to be useless, saying: "There is no benefit in this, and what wisdom demands it?" This, even though the masters of crafts are humans like him, and he could share their crafts and surpass them in them. Then what of the One whose wisdom has dazzled minds, who has no partner in His wisdom, just as He has no partner in His creation, nor any partner in any respect? Whoever thinks he can measure His wisdom with the measure of his intellect, or make his intellect a scale for it, so that what he grasps he takes as near and what he does not grasp he denies, is of the most ignorant of the ignorant. For God, in everything hidden from people, there is a face of wisdom, and in it are numerous wisdoms that cannot be repelled or denied.

So know now that beneath the roots of these hairs is a measure of heat and moisture, which nature required for these hairs to come out upon them. Do you not see that grass grows in the pools of water after the water has dried from them, because of the moisture they have? For this reason these places are among the most moist parts of the body, and they are most receptive to the growth of hair. Nature then pushed those residues and moistures outward, and they became hair. Had they been retained within the body, they would have harmed it and injured its interior. So their discharge is the very interest of the living creature, and their retention happens only through defect and affliction in it. This is like the discharge of menstrual blood from a woman, which is the very interest and perfection of her. For this reason, its retention is due to corruption in nature and deficiency within it. Do you not see that the one from whom hair of the head and beard is withheld after its time has come, how you see him deficient in nature, deficient in creation and weak in constitution? When you witness this in the hair whose wisdom you know in part, why do you not take it into account for the hair whose wisdom is hidden from you?

And He made the saliva flow constantly to the mouth, never ceasing from it, to moisten the throat and the uvula, to ease speech, and to make food slide down. Buqrat (Hippocrates) said: "Moisture in the mouth is the vehicle of nourishment." So reflect on your state when your saliva dries somewhat and the spring of this spring, which is indispensable, diminishes.

(Section)

Then reflect on God's wisdom in the frequent crying of infants and the benefit they derive from it. Physicians and natural philosophers have witnessed the benefit and wisdom of this, and they said: "In the brains of infants there is moisture which, if it remained in their brains, would produce great afflictions. Crying drains this and sends it down from their brains, so their brains grow strong and healthy." Moreover, crying and wailing widen the passages of breath for the infant, open the veins, and strengthen the nerves. How much benefit and interest the infant has in what you hear of his crying and shouting. If this wisdom is in crying, which is caused by the arrival of harmful pain, and you do not know it and it scarcely occurs to you, then likewise the infliction of pain upon infants has, in its causes and its praiseworthy consequences, wisdoms that have remained hidden from most people, and speech about its wisdoms has been confused, like the confusion of ropes, and people have taken various paths in this matter.

One group said: "There is nothing but pure will, bare of wisdom and of a sought-after end." They closed off this door entirely, and whenever they were asked about something, they answered: "He is not asked about what He does." This is indeed one of the truest statements, yet it is not meant to negate God's wisdom, the praiseworthy consequences of His acts, or the ends sought from them. The intent of the verse is to single Him out for divinity and lordship, and that His wisdom is perfect, that none can repel His judgment, and that He is not to be opposed by questioning, because He does nothing in vain, and creates nothing purposelessly. One is questioned about his act only if he deviated from what is right and it had no benefit or use. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead? Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than God, they would have been ruined. Glory be to God, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾ (21:21–23)

How He brought the verse as a denunciation of those who take gods besides Him, which are not equal to Him, yet He put them on a par with Him despite the greatest difference. So His saying ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ affirms the reality of divinity and singles Him out for lordship and divinity. And His saying ﴿but they will be questioned﴾ concerns the condition of those gods taken as divinities, for they are questioned, managed and governed. How then can they be equated with Him, with the greatest distinction between them? This is the context to which the speech was directed. So the Jabriyyah (Determinists), who made this verse a refuge and stronghold for denying His wisdom and for explaining His acts by their praiseworthy ends and sound consequences, [mistook it]. And God is the granter of success to what is right.

Another group said: "The wisdom in His afflicting them is to compensate them in the Hereafter with complete reward." It was said to them: "Reward could have reached them without this affliction." They answered: "The intervention of affliction regarding them is like the intervention of obligations regarding those who are obligated." It was said to them: "This is refuted by you through the affliction of the children of unbelievers." They answered: "We do not say they are in the Fire, as some people have said, for no one enters the Fire except for a sin, and these have no sin." The argument with them on the question of children and the disputes on both sides concerning it is not the place for this. So they were confronted with what they had no answer for: the affliction of their children whose birth and death were decreed upon disbelief, for there is certainly no compensation in this, nor is it a punishment for disbelief, since punishment cannot precede or hasten the offense. Thus they were bewildered at this point, their principles were shaken, and they produced nothing that reason accepts.

A third group said: "If one considers the source of this question, he would know that it is baseless, and that to strain for an answer to it is to impose what is not required. These pains, their consequences and causes are among the necessities of human existence, from which no creature was created free. They are like heat, cold, hunger, thirst, fatigue, exhaustion, sorrow, grief, weakness and incapacity. So the question about the wisdom of the need for food in hunger, the need for drink in thirst, and for sleep and rest in weariness, these pains are among the necessities of human nature from which neither human nor animal is free. Were one stripped of them, he would not be a human but an angel or some other creation. The pains of children are not more difficult than the pains of adults, but since they have become habitual for them, their impact is easy for them. How great is the difference between what the child suffers and what the adult, sound of mind, endures. All of this follows from the requirements of humanity and the necessity of creation. Had He not created it so, it would have been another creation."

They said: "Thus it is seen that when a child is hungry, thirsty, cold or tired, he has been given something that the adult was not tested with. So his affliction by other pains and ailments is like his affliction by hunger, thirst, cold, and that or more. Man, indeed the living creature, was created only in this form of existence."

They said: "If someone asks and says: 'Why was it created thus? Why was it not created with a nature that cannot suffer pain?'"

This is a corrupt question, for God created him in the world of trial and testing, from a weak substance, which is exposed to calamities, and assembled in a composition subject to kinds of pain. He placed in him the four humors without which he cannot subsist, and which cannot exist except through them. These inevitably produce mixing, blending and interaction, in which some seek to dominate others, in quality at times, in quantity at times, and in both at times. This necessarily causes pains. The existence of the necessary without its necessary consequence is impossible. Then He, glorified is He, placed in him powers, desire and will, which necessitate his ceaseless movement and striving to seek what benefits him and to repel what harms him, sometimes by himself and sometimes with the help of others. He made one kind need another, so mixing and intermingling arose among them, and some transgressed against others. From this arose pains and evils, in the manner in which the mixing of his humors and their blending arises, and some of them transgress against others. Pains never fail to accompany this mixture, except in the abode of permanence and enduring bliss, not in the abode of trial and testing. Whoever thinks that wisdom requires the properties of that abode to be placed in this one, has thought falsely. Rather, complete and far-reaching wisdom demanded that this abode be one whose well-being is mixed with its afflictions, whose ease with its toil, whose pleasure with its pains, whose health with its sickness, and whose joy with its sorrow. It is an abode of trial, in which some of its calamities are repelled by others, as the poet said:

I have become in an abode of calamities,
I repel calamities with calamities.

He spoke truly, for when you reflect on eating, drinking, clothing, intercourse, rest and all that is enjoyed, you see that by them one repels the pains and calamities opposed to them. Do you not see that you repel the pain of hunger by eating, the pain of thirst by drinking, and the pain of heat and cold by clothing, and likewise the rest?

From here some wise people said: "Its pleasures for us are only the repelling of pains, nothing more. As for true pleasures, they have another abode and another place, other than this." The existence of these pains and pleasures, mixed and blended, is among the evidences for the Return (ma'ad), and that the wisdom which required this demands, rather, two abodes: an abode purely of pleasure, which no pain whatsoever mixes with, and an abode purely of pain, which no pleasure whatsoever mixes with. The first abode is Paradise and the second is the Fire. Do you not see how this indicates that, given what you are naturally made of in this existence of pleasure and pain, pointing to Paradise and the Fire, and you have seen their signs and evidences of their existence from yourself, so that you almost witness them directly? Consider how witness, sense and existence point to the wisdom of the Lord, exalted is He, and to the truthfulness of His messengers in what they reported of Paradise and the Fire.

Therefore, reflect on how contemplation of God's wisdom has led to the testimony of the intellects and natural dispositions (fitar) to the truthfulness of His messengers and to what they reported in detail, which reason indicates only in summary. Where, then, is this station compared with one who carries his knowledge to the point of opposing what the messengers brought against the proofs and evidences of reason? But those intellects were misled by their Creator, who left them to themselves, so that the armies of abandonment (khudhlan) descended upon them from every side. Let this chapter and its great benefit from this book suffice you. God is the Praised One, the One sought for the perfection of His blessing. These are brief, beneficial words on the question of the suffering of children, which you will likely not find in most books. Now return to yourself and reflect on these natural acts placed within the human being, and on the wisdom and benefit in them, and on what has been given to each of them in its bare nature, and the motive that it requires and urges. Hunger urges eating and seeks it, because of what it contains of sustenance for the body and its life and its death. Drowsiness requires sleep and urges it, because of what it contains of rest for the body and its limbs, and of restoring the powers and returning them to their strength renewed, not exhausted. Sexual desire requires intercourse, through which offspring continue and the need is fulfilled and pleasure is completed. You find these motives driving the human being toward these matters and demanding them from him without his choice, and that is the very essence of wisdom. For if the human being only summoned these urges when he willed, he would almost be occupied away from them by whatever afflictions befell him for a period, so his body would waste away, perish, and tend toward corruption while he is unaware, just as when his body needs some medicine and remedy, and he repels it and turns away from it, until the disease takes hold of him and destroys him. So the wisdom of the Subtle, the All-Aware, required that He place within him impulses and urgings that drive him strongly toward what contains his sustenance, his survival, and his welfare, and that return to him without his choice or his summoning. Thus He made for each of these acts a motive from the very nature of the disposition, which moves it and urges him toward it. Then look at what He has given him of the various powers by which his sustenance is maintained. He gave the attractive power, which seeks and urges toward its known nourishment, so it takes it and delivers it to the limbs according to their capacity to receive it. Then He gave the retentive power, which holds the food and keeps it until nature ripens it, perfects its cooking, prepares it for its uses, and dispatches it to whoever deserves it. Then He gave the digestive power, which transforms it within the body and digests it in the stomach. Then He gave the expulsive power, which expels its heaviness and whatever has no benefit in it, so it pushes it out of the body so that it does not harm or weaken him. So who gave you this power at the moment of your greatest need for it? Who made it your servant? Who gave it its functions, and made each of them operate differently from the others, and joined them together despite their diversity, until they were gathered in one person and one locus? Had they been at odds with one another, some of them would have destroyed the others. Who is it that stands between you and that? Were it not for the attractive power, how would you be moved to seek the nourishment by which the body subsists? Were it not for the retentive power, how would the food remain in the belly until the stomach digests it? Were it not for the digestive power, how would it be cooked until its pure essence reached all parts of the body and its depths? Were it not for the expulsive power, how would the harmful, deadly heaviness, if it were retained, be expelled little by little, so that the body would rest, become light, and become active? Reflect, then, on how this power has been entrusted to you and charged with your welfare. The body is like the house of a king, in which there are his attendants and servants, and in charge of that house are stewards who maintain its affairs: some for meeting its needs and bringing provisions to it, some for receiving what comes in and keeping it until it is prepared and refined, some for receiving it, preparing it, and delivering it to the people of the house, distributing it among them according to their needs, and some for sweeping the house, cleaning it, and clearing it of refuse and filth. The King is the true, manifest King, may His majesty be exalted, the house is you, the attendants and servants are the limbs and organs, and those who oversee them are these powers we have mentioned.

Note: There is a difference between the view of the physician and the naturalist regarding these matters. Their examination of them is confined to preserving health and repelling sickness, so they look at them only from this aspect. The view of the believer who knows God through them is different: he looks at them from the aspect of their indication of their Creator and Originator, and of the profound wisdoms, abundant blessings, and favours in them, which call the servants to thank Him and remember Him.

(Note)

Then reflect on the wisdom of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in memory and forgetfulness, which He has specifically granted to the human species, and what wisdoms are in them and what benefits the servant has in them. For were it not for the power of retention with which he was endowed, disorder would enter all his affairs. He would not know what he owns or what is owed to him, nor what he took or gave, nor what he heard or saw, nor what he said or what was said to him, nor who did him good or who wronged him, nor who was his associate, so that he would draw near to whoever benefits him, or distance himself from whoever harms him. Then he would not be guided to the path he took the first time even if he took it many times, nor would he know a science even if he studied it all his life, nor would he benefit from experience, nor could he take a lesson from what has passed. Rather, he would be on the verge of stripping away his humanity entirely.

So reflect on the great benefit to you in these faculties, and on the place of each one of them, let alone all of them together.

Among the most wondrous blessings bestowed upon him is the blessing of forgetfulness. For were it not for forgetfulness, he would not be consoled over anything, nor would any grief come to an end for him, nor would he be consoled for any calamity, nor would any sorrow die in him, nor would any resentment vanish from him, nor would he enjoy any of the goods of this world while remembering its afflictions, nor would he hope for the heedlessness of an enemy or for the misfortune of an envier. So reflect on the blessing of God in memory and forgetfulness, though they differ and oppose each other, and on His making in each of them a kind of benefit.

(Note)

Then reflect on this disposition with which the human being is specifically endowed above all animals: the disposition of modesty (hayaʾ), which is among the best and most noble of morals, greatest in worth and most abundant in benefit. Indeed, it is the distinguishing mark of humanity. Whoever lacks modesty has nothing of humanity with him except flesh, blood, and an outward form, just as he has nothing of goodness with him. Were it not for this disposition, a person would not host a guest, nor fulfil a promise, nor return a trust, nor meet anyone's need, nor seek out the beautiful person to prefer him or avoid the ugly one, nor would he cover his nakedness, nor refrain from indecency. And many people, were it not for the modesty within them, would not perform any of the duties incumbent upon them, nor would they respect the rights of any creature, nor would they maintain ties of kinship, nor show kindness to a parent.

The motive for these acts is either religious, which is the hope for their praiseworthy outcome, or worldly and lofty, which is the modesty of the doer before the creatures. It has become clear that were it not for modesty, whether before the Creator or before the creatures, the doer would not perform them.

In al-Tirmidhi and others, it is related with a raised (marfuʿ) chain:

"Be modest before God with the modesty due to Him."

They said: "And what is the due modesty?"

He said: "That you guard the head and what it contains, and the belly and what it holds, and that you remember the graves and decay."

And he said: "If you have no modesty, then do what you wish."

The most correct of the two views concerning it is that of Abu ʿUbayd and the majority, that it is a warning, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do what you will﴾, and His saying, ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little﴾.

Another group said it is permission and license, meaning: when you want to do an act, look before doing it. If it is something of which one should be modest before God and before people, do not do it. If it is something of which one need not be modest, do it, for it is not ugly. In my view, however, this statement has the form of a command but its meaning is that of a report, and it is equivalent to the saying, "Whoever has no modesty does what he desires." It is therefore neither permission nor mere warning, but has the sense of a report. The meaning is that what restrains one from ugliness is modesty, so whoever has no modesty will do as he pleases. Expressing this meaning in the form of a command is for a very wondrous subtlety, namely that the human being has two commanders and two restrainers: a commander and restrainer from the side of modesty, so when he obeys it he refrains from doing whatever he desires, and a commander and restrainer from the side of desire and nature. Whoever does not obey the commander and restrainer of modesty will inevitably obey the commander of desire and passion. So expressing the statement in the mould of a command conveys this meaning, which would not be conveyed by saying, "Whoever has no modesty does what he desires."

(Note)

Then reflect on God's blessing upon the human being with the two kinds of eloquence: the spoken eloquence and the written eloquence. He, glorified is He, has counted these among the blessings He bestowed upon His servant. He said at the beginning of the surah revealed to the Messenger of God:

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know﴾.

Reflect on how He gathered in these words all the stages of creation, and how they contain the four stages of existence in the most concise, clear, and beautiful expression. He first mentioned the generality of creation, which is the bestowal of external existence. Then He mentioned the particularity of the creation of man, because it is the locus of lessons and signs, and there are great signs in him, and from witnessing them comes the pure multiplicity of blessings. Here He mentioned the material of his creation as a clinging substance (ʿalaqah), whereas elsewhere He mentions what precedes it, either the material of the root, which is dust and clay, or the sounding clay like pottery, or the material of the branch, which is the despised water.

In this passage He mentioned the first beginning of the connection of creation, which is the clinging substance, for before it there was a drop, and its first transformation is into the clinging substance. Then He mentioned, third, teaching by the pen, which is among the greatest of His blessings upon His servants, for by it sciences are preserved, rights are established, precepts are learned, testimonies are guarded, and the accounts of transactions among people are kept. By it the reports of the past are fixed for those who come after. Were it not for writing, the reports of some ages would be cut off from others, the sunan would be effaced, rulings would be confused, and later generations would not know the ways of earlier ones. Most of the corruption entering people's religion and worldly affairs comes from forgetfulness, which erases the forms of knowledge from their hearts. So He gave them the book as a vessel that protects knowledge from loss, like the containers that protect goods from being destroyed and wasted. Thus the blessing of God, mighty and majestic, in teaching by the pen, after the Qur'an, is among the greatest blessings. Teaching by it, although a person may reach it through cleverness and stratagem, is a gift God bestowed from Himself and a grace He granted and an increase in His creation and bounty. It is He who taught him writing, and although he is the one who learns, his act is the act of one responding to the teaching of the One who taught by the pen. For He taught him, and he learned, just as He taught him speech, and so he speaks. Who gave you the mind by which you understand, the tongue by which you express, and the fingers by which you write? Who prepared your mind to accept this teaching above all other animals? Who made your tongue speak and your fingers move? Who strengthened the fingers with the palm and the palm with the forearm? How many signs of God there are that we are heedless of in learning by the pen! So pause for a moment while writing.

Consider your state as you hold the pen, which is inanimate, and place it upon the paper, which is inanimate, so that from their union arise kinds of wisdom, varieties of knowledge, forms of correspondence, sermons, verse, prose, and answers to questions. Who caused the meanings to flow onto your heart and imprinted them in your mind? Then who caused the expressions that indicate them to flow onto your tongue, then moved your fingers with them until they became a wondrous design whose meaning is more wondrous than its form? Through it you accomplish your aims, reach a need in your breast, and send it to distant lands and far regions, where it stands in your place, speaks on your behalf, speaks with your tongue, takes the place of your messenger, and benefits you in ways that a messenger you send could not, for He is the One who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.

Teaching by the pen involves three stages: the stage of mental existence, the stage of verbal existence, and the stage of written existence. The teaching by the pen indicates that He, glorified is He, is the Giver of these stages, and His saying "created" indicates that He gives external existence. These verses, despite their brevity, conciseness, and eloquence, show that all stages of existence are ascribed to Him, exalted is He: ﴿creation and teaching﴾, and He mentioned two kinds of creation and two kinds of teaching: general creation and particular creation, and particular teaching and general teaching. Among His attributes here He mentioned the Most Generous, in whom is every good and every perfection. So He possesses every perfection in attribute, and from Him comes every good in act.
