He is the Most Generous in His essence, His attributes, and His acts. This creation and teaching arose only from His generosity, kindness, and beneficence, not from any need that compelled Him to it, for He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praised.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an. He created man. He taught him the expression [al-bayan]﴾.

These words indicate His, glorified is He, giving all stages of existence. His saying "He created man" is a report of external, concrete existence, and He specified man for creation because of what has preceded. His saying "He taught the Qur'an" is a report of the giving of mental, knowledgeable existence, for man learns the Qur'an only through His teaching, just as he became a human being only through His creating him. So He is the One who created him and taught him. Then He said: ﴿He taught him the expression﴾.

Al-bayan (expression, clarity) encompasses three stages, each of which is called bayan. The first is mental bayan, by which one distinguishes between known matters. The second is verbal bayan, by which one expresses those known matters and conveys them to another. The third is written bayan, the inscribed form in which those words are drawn, so that the viewer understands their meanings just as the listener understands the meanings of words. The first is clarity to the heart; the second is clarity to the hearing; the third is clarity to the sight. God often combines these three, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart, all of these will be questioned about﴾, and His saying: ﴿And God brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight, and hearts, that perhaps you would give thanks﴾.

And he censures those who do not benefit from these faculties in acquiring guidance and beneficial knowledge, as in His saying ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ and His saying ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their sight is a veil﴾. This discussion has already been expounded upon, as a reminder. Then reflect on the wisdom of the Subtle, the All-Aware: in what He gave man knowledge of what is good for his livelihood and his return (to his Lord), and withheld from him knowledge of what he has no need of. So his ignorance of it does no harm, and his knowledge of it benefits him not at all. Then He made easy for him the paths to the knowledge he needs, with the utmost ease; and the greater his need for a given knowledge, the more complete its facilitation for him. So He gave him knowledge of his Creator, Originator and Inventor, glory be to Him, and acknowledgment of Him, and made easy for him the paths to this knowledge. There is no knowledge more sublime than it, nor more evident to reason and innate nature, and there are no paths to knowledge by which one attains more, nor more indicative, clearer or more manifest. Whatever you see with your eye, hear with your ear, comprehend with your heart, whatever occurs to your mind, and whatever any of your senses reaches, is a sign pointing to the Lord, blessed and exalted. Thus the paths to knowledge of the Maker are innate and necessary; there is no knowledge more manifest than them. Every proof offered for the Maker, knowledge of His existence is more evident than the proof itself. For this reason the Messengers said to their peoples, ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾, addressing them in a manner suited only to one in whose mind no doubt about the existence of God, glory be to Him, should arise. He established, for His existence, His oneness and the attributes of His perfection, proofs of various kinds, which none can enumerate except God. Then He embedded this in the innate nature and placed it in the intellect as a whole, then sent the Messengers as reminders of it. For this reason the Exalted says, ﴿So remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾, and His saying ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾, and His saying ﴿You are only a reminder﴾, and His saying ﴿Why are they turning away from the reminder?﴾
This is abundant in the Qur'an, and details what is in the innate nature and intellect in summary. So consider how acknowledgment of Him, of His oneness, of the attributes of His perfection, the qualities of His majesty, His wisdom in creation and in command, which necessitate the affirmation of the mission of His messengers, and the recompense of the good-doer for his goodness and the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing, was deposited in the innate nature and fixed within it. Had it been left as He created it, nothing would have come upon it to corrupt it, alter it, or change it from what it was made upon; it would have affirmed His oneness, the obligation to thank and obey Him, His attributes, His wisdom in His acts, and reward and punishment. But when it became corrupt and deviated from the path upon which it was created, it denied what it denied and rejected what it rejected. So God sent His messengers as reminders to the people of sound and upright natures, and they submitted willingly, by choice, in love and in acceptance, by what He had placed as evidence of this in their hearts, to the point that some of them did not ask about the miracle or the extraordinary sign, but knew the truth of the call from its very essence, and knew that it is a true call whose proof is within it. And (the messengers were) admonishing and establishing clear evidence against the people of corrupt natures, lest they argue against God that He did not guide them or show them the way, so that the word would be justified against them by the establishment of the proof. Thus He, glory be to Him, would not be unjust to them by punishing and wretching them. God has clarified this in His saying ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an, to warn whoever is alive and that the word may be justified against the disbelievers﴾.
So reflect on how the knowledge of God, the testimony to His oneness, the affirmation of His names and attributes, the mission of His messengers and the resurrection for recompense, are inscribed and established in the innate natures. One would not know that they are firmly rooted in his nature until the messengers remind him and alert him; then, when they tell him what he already has, he sees what they told him settled in his nature, testified to by his intellect and even by his limbs and the tongue of his state. This is the greatest form of faith, and it is what He, glory be to Him, wrote in the hearts of His friends and elect, as He said, ﴿Those—He has written faith in their hearts﴾. So ponder this section, for it is one of the treasures of this book, and it deserves that fingers be folded in praise of it. And to God belongs all praise and grace.
The purpose is that God, glory be to Him, gave the servant of these knowledges and their paths, and made them easy for him, what He did not give him of other things, due to the great need of his livelihood and return for them. Then He placed in the intellect, of acknowledgment of the goodness of His law and religion, which is His shadow on earth, His justice among His servants, and His light in the world, what if the intellects of all the worlds were gathered together, and they were upon the intellect of the most intelligent man among them, they could not propose anything better than it, nor more just, nor more righteous, nor more beneficial for creation in its livelihood and return.
So it is His greatest sign and clearest proof, and His most manifest argument that He is God, there is no god but Him, and that He is characterized by every perfection and free from every defect and likeness. Far more so, it needs no witness from outside to establish it by proofs and evidences, to multiply the paths of guidance, to cut off excuse, and to remove the cause and doubt: ﴿That whoever perishes may perish by clear proof, and whoever lives may live by clear proof. And indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ (8:42).
So He established in the innate nature the goodness of justice, fairness, truthfulness, righteousness, benevolence, fulfilling covenants, sincere counsel to creation, mercy to the needy, support of the oppressed, consolation of those in need and want, returning trusts, repaying goodness with goodness and evil with pardon and forgiveness, patience in the places of patience, generosity in the places of giving, retribution in the place of retribution, forbearance in the place of forbearance, tranquility, dignity, compassion, gentleness, deliberateness, good character, and fine companionship with relatives and strangers, covering faults, pardoning slips, preferring others in times of need, relieving distress, dispelling calamities, cooperating in all kinds of good and righteousness, courage, generosity, insight, steadfastness, resolve, strength in truth and gentleness toward its people, severity toward the people of falsehood and harshness toward them, reconciling between people and striving to set right the relations between them, honoring whoever deserves honor and humiliating whoever deserves humiliation, placing people in their (proper) ranks, and giving every rightful person his right, and (it established) taking what is made easy for them and what their souls are disposed to of deeds, wealth and character; and (it established) guiding their astray, teaching their ignorant, bearing with their harshness, and equality of near and far in right, so that the one nearest to it is the most worthy of the truth even if he is far, and the one farthest from it is the farthest from the truth even if he is beloved and near; and so on, of knowledge of the intellect that He placed among them in dealings, marriages and crimes, and what He deposited in their natures of the goodness of thanking and worshipping Him alone with no partner, and that His favors upon them require spending their power and capacity in thanking Him, drawing near to Him, and preferring Him over all else. He also established in the natures their knowledge of the ugliness of the opposites of these, then sent His messengers to command what He had established in the natures as good and perfect, and to forbid what He had established in them as ugly, defective and blameworthy.
So the revealed Law agreed with the perfecting natural disposition in full agreement in its details and totality, and the evidences of His religion in the natural disposition stood calling to faith, "Come to success," and those signs and proofs shattered the darkness of the fathers' oppression, as the light of morning shatters the night. And the Law's judge accepted the testimony of intellect and natural disposition, since the witness is not suspect nor exposed to injury.

The provision and what you are promised are in the heaven. Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Tafsir al-Qayyim*, commentary on surah 51, verses 22–23:

As for the provision (al-rizq), it has been explained as rain, as Paradise, and as the provision of this world and the next. There is no doubt that rain is part of mercy, and that Paradise is the abode of mercy. So the provision of both abodes is in the heaven, which is above. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and what you are promised﴾: ʿAṭāʾ said, "It is the reward and the punishment." Al-Kalbī said, "It is the good and the evil." Mujāhid said, "It is Paradise and Hell." Ibn Sīrīn said, "It is the matter of the Hour."

I say: That Paradise and good are in the heaven presents no difficulty. That Hell is in the heaven, and what its people are promised, requires clarification. When you consider the causes of good and evil, the causes of entering Paradise and Hell, and the division and separation of people into wretched and blessed, you find all of that by the decree and predestination of God, which descends from the heaven. All of that is recorded in the heaven, in the scrolls of the angels and in the Preserved Tablet, before the deed and after it. So the entire matter is from the heaven. The statement of the one who said "the matter of the Hour" reveals this meaning, for the matter of the Hour comes from the heaven, and it is what is promised with it. Paradise and Hell are the ultimate end for which the Hour was established. So every statement of the early generations (al-salaf, the pious predecessors) on this is correct, and God knows best.

(Section)

Then He swore the greatest oath by the greatest thing sworn by, concerning the most important matter sworn about, and He emphasized the report with this oath. Then He emphasized it further by likening it to a matter that is established and that no one of sound perception doubts. So He said, ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as [certainly as] you speak.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "He means it is a true, occurring reality, just as you speak." Al-Farrāʾ said, "It is true, just as a human being is speaking." Al-Zajjāj said, "This is like when you say in speech: 'Indeed this is true, just as you are here.'"

I say: In a hadith there is also: "It is true, just as you are here." So God likened the certainty of what He reported to the certainty of human speech and its existence. Each of us knows by necessity that he speaks, and his speech does not need proof of its existence, and no doubt about his speaking occurs to him. Likewise, what God has reported about the matter of tawḥīd (monotheism), prophethood (nubuwwah), the return (maʿād, the resurrection and final return), and His names and attributes, is a truth established in reality, likened to the establishment of your speech and existence. This is a principle people know in their speech; one of them says, "This is true like the sun." The poet made this clear with his words:

"Nothing is sound in the minds
when daylight needs a proof."

Here is a matter that should be noticed: the Lord, exalted is He, testified to the truth of what He reported, and He is the most truthful of the truthful. He swore to it, and He is the most faithful of those who swear. He emphasized it by likening it to what is actual and admits no doubt in any way. He established upon it visible and demonstrative proofs that made it witnessed and seen by insight, even if not seen by the eyes. Yet most souls are heedless of it. They are not prepared for it and do not take provision for it. Only the one who prepares for it and takes provision for it gives it its due, and such people are only a single individual after another. Most of creation does not reflect on the purpose of their being created and brought into this abode, nor do they reflect on the brevity of their stay in the abode of deception, nor on their departure and transfer from it, nor where they are going or where they will settle. Sensation has dominated them, their share of intellect is little, heedlessness has overtaken them, the desires that are like a mirage have deceived them, and long hope has tricked them. It is as if the one who stays will never leave, as if one of them will never be resurrected or questioned, and as if with every resident there is a decree from God to so-and-so son of so-and-so granting safety from His punishment and success in His abundant reward. As for sensual pleasures and soul-desires, however they are obtained, they obtain them, and from whatever direction they appear they seize them, heedless of being held to account, secure from the consequence. They strive for what they attain and leave what they are responsible for. They build what they will leave and ruin what they will arrive at. They are heedless of the Hereafter. The desires of their souls have distracted them, so they do not look into what benefits those souls, nor do they take up gathering provision for their journey. ﴿They forgot God, so He caused them to forget themselves. Those are the defiant ones.﴾

The utmost wonder is at the heedlessness of one whose breaths are counted for him and whose moments are numbered, while the mounts of night and day are hastening him along, yet he does not reflect where he is being carried or to what station he is being taken:

"How can the eye sleep, content,
when it does not know in which of the two abodes it will descend?"

When death comes upon one of them, he grows anxious over the ruin of his self and the loss of his pleasures, not because of his past sins, nor because of the evil of his final destination after death. If a thought of that occurs to one of them, he relies on pardon or mercy, and he is certain that this is his share and that it is inevitable. If the intelligent person were to bring his mind into focus, to employ his intellect, to direct his thought, to look deeply, and to reflect on the signs in order to understand the purpose of his creation, then the eye of the traveler would look at the road, the wayfarer would take provision, the sick person would seek treatment, and the prudent person would prepare for what might come. How much more so for a matter that is certain, given the sincerity of his faith and the strength of their certainty, as if they were witnessing the matter. Thus the dwelling places of faith have become empty of their people, and its landmarks lie ruined upon their foundations.

Ibn Wahb said: Muslim ibn ʿAlī informed me, from al-Awzāʿī, who said: "When the dawn rose, or just before it, the early generations (al-salaf) were as if birds were upon their heads, turned toward themselves. Even if a beloved of one of them had been absent from him for a while and then returned, he would not turn to him. They would remain like that until sunrise. Then some of them would stand up to others, and they would start with the first thing that pertains to the matter of their return and what they are heading toward. Then they would turn to jurisprudence (fiqh)."

(Benefit: On the singular form of "the heaven")

Consider how [the word "the heaven" (al-samāʾ)] came in the singular in His words: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as [certainly as] you speak.﴾

It is intended to cover these two kinds. That is, the Lord of everything above and everything below. Since the intention is the generality of His lordship, He used the term that includes everything that is called a heaven and everything that is called an earth.

This is a real matter that does not change or alter, even if the very heavens and earths are transformed. Notice how [the word "heavens" (al-samāwāt)] came in the plural in His words: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth glorifies God.﴾

In every case, since the intention was to report the glorification of their inhabitants in their multitude and the difference of their ranks, it was necessary to use the plural for their places.

Notice how it came in the singular in His words: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised.﴾

The provision is rain, and what we are promised is Paradise, and both are in this direction, not that each one is in each individual heaven. So the singular form was more fitting for it.

(Admonition)

Empty your heart for the concern you have been commanded with, and do not occupy it with what has been guaranteed to you, for provision and term of life are two guaranteed partners. As long as the term remains, the provision will come.

When He closes off one of its avenues to you by His wisdom, He opens for you by His mercy an avenue better for you than it.

Consider the state of the fetus. Its nourishment, which is blood, comes to it through one channel, the umbilical cord. When it emerges from its mother's womb and that channel is cut off, He opens for it two channels and provides for it, through them, a better and more delicious provision than the first: pure, palatable milk. When the period of nursing is complete and the two channels are cut off by weaning, He opens four channels, more complete: two foods and two drinks. The two foods are from animals and plants, and the two drinks are from water and milk, along with what is added to them of benefits and pleasures.

When he dies, these four channels are cut off from him. But He, glorified is He, if he was blessed, opens for him eight channels, which are the eight gates of Paradise, through which he enters from whichever he wishes.

Thus the Lord, glorified is He, does not withhold from His believing servant anything of this world except that He gives him something better than it and more beneficial for him. This is not the case for the non-believer, for He withholds from him the lowest, meanest share, and does not approve it for him, so that He may give him the highest, most precious share.

The servant, because of his ignorance of the interests of his own soul and his ignorance of his Lord's generosity, wisdom, and kindness, does not recognize the difference between what was withheld from him and what was stored up for him. Rather, he is fixated on love of the immediate, even if it is lowly, and has little desire for the deferred, even if it is exalted.

If the servant were just toward his Lord (and how could he be?), he would know that His favor upon him in what He withheld from him of the world and its pleasures and bliss is greater than His favor upon him in what He gave him of that. He withheld nothing except to give, did not test him except to grant him well-being, did not try him except to purify his bond with Him, did not cause him to die except to give him life, and did not bring him out to this abode except to prepare himself from it for meeting Him and to take the path that leads to Him. So ﴿He made the night and the day alternating for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful﴾, and ﴿the wrongdoers refused except ingratitude﴾. And God is the One sought for help.

Therefore in this there is praise of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) from several aspects.

The first of them: that He described his guests as "honoured" (mukramun).

This is according to one of two opinions:

That it refers to Ibrahim's honouring of them.

The second: that they are the honoured ones in the sight of Allah.

There is no contradiction between the two opinions: the verse indicates both meanings.

The second: His saying, ﴿when they entered upon him﴾, without mentioning their seeking permission to enter.

In this is evidence that he (ﷺ) was known for honouring guests and for the habit of hosting them.

So his house became a place of hospitality, frequented by whoever came to it. He had no need to ask permission, and the entry of one who came in was itself his permission. This is the utmost of generosity.

The third: His saying ﴿Peace (salamun)﴾ in the nominative. They had greeted him with the accusative, ﴿Peace (salaman)﴾.

The nominative salam is more complete, because it indicates the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), which signifies permanence and renewal, whereas the accusative indicates the verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya), which signifies occurrence and renewal.

Thus Abraham greeted them with a greeting better than theirs.

Their saying ﴿salaman﴾ means "we greet with a greeting," whereas his saying ﴿salam﴾ means "peace be upon you."

The fourth: He omitted the subject (mubtada') in his saying ﴿a people unknown﴾. When he did not recognise them and did not know them, he was shy to confront them with a word that would repel the guest, such as saying "you are honoured." So omitting the subject here is among the most refined forms of speech.

The fifth: He put the verb into the passive and omitted its agent, saying ﴿unknown﴾ and not saying "I honour you."

This is better in this context, and further from repelling them or confronting them with harshness.

[A discussion on responding to one who says "wa-'alaykum al-salam" (and upon you be peace), and the difference between it and the response to the People of the Book]

He used to respond to one who greeted him with "wa-'alaykum al-salam" (and upon you be peace), with the waw, and with placing "'alaykum" before the word "al-salam".

People have disputed here a question: if the one responding drops the waw and says "'alaykum al-salam", would this be valid? A group, including al-Mutawalli and others, said: it is not a response, and the obligation of responding is not fulfilled by it, because it contradicts the Sunnah of responding, and because it is not known whether it is a response or the initiating of a greeting, since its form is suitable for both. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the People of the Book greet you, say: 'wa-'alaykum' (and upon you)." This is a reminder from him of the obligation of the waw in responding to the people of Islam, since the waw in such a phrase establishes the first statement and affirms the second. If he was commanded to use the waw in responding to the People of the Book, who say "al-sam 'alaykum", and he said "When the People of the Book greet you, say: 'wa-'alaykum'", then mentioning it in responding to Muslims is more fitting and more deserving.

Another group held that it is a valid response, just as if it had the waw. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) affirmed this in his large book, and argued for this view with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Has there reached you the story of the honoured guests of Abraham? When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 24-25].

That is: "peace be upon you." This is necessary, but omission was good in the response for the sake of the omission in the initiating greeting. They also argued with what is in the two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah created Adam, his height sixty cubits. When He had created him, He said to him: 'Go and greet that group of angels, and listen to what they greet you with, for it will be your greeting and the greeting of your descendants.' He said, 'Peace be upon you.' They said, 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah,' and they added to him: 'and the mercy of Allah.'" So the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that this is his greeting and the greeting of his descendants.

They said: Also, the one greeted is commanded to greet the one who greets him with a greeting like his, as a matter of justice (adl), and with a better one as a matter of grace (fadl). So when he responds with a greeting like his, he has done what is just.

As for his saying, "When the People of the Book greet you, say: 'wa-'alaykum'," this hadith has differing narrations regarding the word "waw" in it. It is narrated in three ways, the first of which is with the waw.

Abu Dawud said: Thus did Malik narrate it from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, and al-Thawri narrated it from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, saying in it: "fa-'alaykum" (so upon you). The hadith of Sufyan in the two Sahihs. Al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Uyayna from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar with the waw dropped. In a wording in Muslim and al-Nasa'i: "Say 'alayka' (upon you) without a waw."

Al-Khattabi said: Most of the hadith scholars narrate it as "wa-'alaykum" with the waw, while Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated it as "'alaykum" with the waw dropped, and this is the correct version. That is because when the waw is dropped, their very saying which they said is returned to them, whereas with the waw there is sharing with them and entering into what they said, because the waw is a particle of conjunction and of joining two things. End of his words.

What he mentioned about the waw is not problematic. Most scholars hold that "al-sam" means death, and both the one greeting and the one greeted share in it. So the presence of the waw clarifies the non-exclusivity and affirms participation, while its omission indicates that the greeter is more deserving of it and more entitled to it than the one greeted. On this basis, the presence of the waw is the correct form and is better than omitting it, as narrated by Malik and others. However, "al-sam" has been interpreted as "al-sa'ama," which means weariness and the weariness of religion. They said: On this basis the correct form is to drop the waw, without exception. But this contradicts the familiar meaning of this word in the language. That is why it came in the hadith: "Indeed the black seed is a cure for every disease except al-sam," and they do not differ that it means death.

Some pretentious people (al-mutahadhlaqin) have gone so far as to say that he should respond to them with "al-salam" with a kasra on the sin, meaning stones, the plural of salima. Refuting this response is itself required.

[Chapter: On his guidance (ﷺ) regarding greeting the People of the Book]

It is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said:

"Do not initiate greeting them with salam, and when you meet them on the road, force them to the narrowest part of the road."

However, it has been said that this was in a specific circumstance, when they marched against Banu Qurayza, and he said: "Do not initiate greeting them with salam."

So is this a general ruling for the protected people (ahl al-dhimma, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule) absolutely, or is it restricted to those whose condition is like the condition of those people? This is a matter for consideration. However, Muslim narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"Do not initiate greeting the Jews or the Christians with salam, and when you meet one of them on the road, force him to its narrowest part."

The apparent meaning is that this is a general ruling.

The early scholars (al-salaf) and later scholars (al-khalaf) differed on this. Most of them said: they are not to be initiated with salam. Others held that it is permissible to initiate greeting them, just as they are responded to. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Umama, and Ibn Muhayriz, and it is an opinion in the school of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him). However, the proponent of this view said: one says to him only "al-salam 'alayka" without mentioning mercy, and in the singular. A group said: initiating is permissible for a prevailing benefit, such as a need one has of him, or fear of his harm, or a kinship between them, or a cause that requires it. This was narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and 'Alqama.

Al-Awza'i said: If you greet, then the righteous have greeted, and if you leave it, then the righteous have left it.

They differed concerning the obligation of responding to them. The majority hold that it is obligatory, and this is the correct view. Another group said: responding to them is not obligatory, just as it is not obligatory for the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'a), and even more so. The correct view is the first, and the difference is that we are commanded to shun the people of innovation, as a means of disciplining them and warning against them, unlike the protected people.

It is established from him (ﷺ) that he "passed by a gathering in which there were a mixture of Muslims, polytheists who worshipped idols, and Jews, and he greeted them with salam."

And it is authentically reported from him that "he wrote to Heraclius and others: 'Peace be upon him who follows the guidance.'"

Sixth: that he turned aside to his family to bring them a meal for his guests.

Ruagan (turning aside secretly) is going off in such a way that one almost is not noticed. This is from the generosity of the host: that he withdraws in concealment so that the guest does not notice, which would otherwise burden and embarrass him. The guest only becomes aware of it when the food has already come to him, unlike one who hears his host say to him, or to those present, "Stay where you are until I bring you the food," and the like, which causes the guest shame and discomfort.

Seventh: that he went to his family and brought the hospitality.

This indicates that such provision was ready and prepared among them for guests. He did not need to go to others, such as his neighbours or anyone else, to buy it or borrow it.

Eighth: his saying, "Then he brought a fat calf" (﴿فَجَاءَ بِعِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ﴾), indicates that he served the guest himself.

He did not say, "He ordered for them," but rather he himself went and brought it personally, and did not send it with his servant.

This is more eloquent in honouring the guest.

Ninth: that he brought a whole calf, and did not bring merely a piece of it.

This is from the completeness of his generosity (ﷺ).

Tenth: that it was fat, not lean. It is known that this was among the finest of their wealth, and such an animal is kept for breeding and rearing, yet he preferred it for his guests.

The eleventh point: that he brought it (the food) close to them himself, and did not order his servant to do so.

The twelfth point: that he brought it close to them, and did not bring them close to it.

This is more eloquent in showing honour: that you seat the guest and then bring the food close to him, carrying it to his presence, and not place the food in a corner and then order your guest to come near it.

The thirteenth point: that he said, "Will you not eat?"

This is an offering and a gentle manner of speech, and it is better than saying "Eat," or "Stretch out your hands," or the like.

This is among the things people recognise by their intellects as good and gracious.

For this reason they say: "In the name of God," or "Will you not give charity?" or "Will you not be made whole?" and similar phrases.

The fourteenth point: that he only offered them the food because he saw that they were not eating. His guests did not need his permission to eat; rather, whenever he set food before them, they would eat. But these guests, when they refrained from eating, he said to them, "Will you not eat?"

For this reason, "he felt a fear of them (awjasa minhum khifah)," meaning he sensed it and concealed it within himself, and did not show it to them. And this is:

The fifteenth point: when they refrained from eating his food, he feared them, and did not show them his fear.

When the angels perceived this from him, they said, "Do not fear," and gave him the glad tidings of a forbearing boy.

Thus this verse has gathered the etiquettes of hospitality, which are the most noble of etiquettes. As for everything else of extra formalities, which are affectation and artifice, they are merely among the customs and habits of people.

And these etiquettes are sufficient as a source of nobility and pride.

So may God send blessings upon our Prophet, and upon Abraham, and upon the family of both of them, and upon all the prophets.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 51, verse 29:

This shows the weakness of a woman's intellect and her lack of steadiness, for she hastened to lament and struck her face at this news.

And her saying ﴿an old woman, barren﴾ shows the good manners of a woman when addressing men, and her restraint in speech to what the need requires. For she omitted the subject and did not say "I am an old woman, barren," and she limited herself to mentioning the cause that indicates she cannot bear children, mentioning nothing else. As for in Surah Hud, she mentioned the obstacle preventing it for her and for Ibrahim, and she expressed amazement explicitly.

And His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿They said, "Thus says your Lord"﴾ includes the affirmation of the attribute of speech for Him.

And His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ includes the affirmation of the attributes of wisdom (hikmah) and knowledge, which are the source of creation and command. Everything that He created proceeds from His knowledge and wisdom, and likewise His command and His legislation (shar') proceed from His knowledge and wisdom.

Knowledge and wisdom include all the attributes of perfection. Knowledge includes life and its necessary perfections: self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah), power, permanence, hearing, sight, and the rest of the attributes that complete knowledge requires. Wisdom includes perfection of will, justice, mercy, benevolence, generosity, and goodness, the placing of things in their proper places in the best of their forms, and it includes the sending of messengers and the establishment of reward and punishment.

All of this is from His name al-Hakim (the All-Wise), as is the method of the Qur'an in establishing these great matters through the attribute of wisdom, and in refuting those who claim that He created creation in vain, purposeless, and without truth. Thus the attribute of His wisdom includes the legislation (shar'), the decree (qadar), reward, and punishment. For this reason, the more correct of the two opinions is that the return (ma'ad, the resurrection) is known by reason, and that revelation (sam') came with the details of what reason indicates.

Whoever reflects on the method of the Qur'an will find it indicating this. He, glory be to Him, sets forth for them rational examples that show the possibility of the return at one time and its occurrence at another. He mentions the proofs of power that indicate the possibility of the return, and the proofs of wisdom that necessitate its occurrence.

Whoever reflects on the proofs of the return in the Qur'an will find them likewise, by the praise of Allah, sufficient in themselves without need of others, adequate and healing, leading to the sought goal swiftly, and including the answer to the doubts that occur to many people.

If success is granted, I would write a great volume on this, given what I have seen in the proofs to which the Qur'an guides, of healing and guidance, swiftness in bringing about conviction, excellence of explanation, and drawing attention to the places of doubt and answering them in a way that soothes the breast and increases certainty. This differs from other proofs, which are the reverse of that. But this is not the place for detail.

(A subtle point: on the use of the word "woman" rather than "wife.")

Al-Suhayli said: Mentioning "the woman" (al-mar'ah) is more fitting in this place, because it is in the context of mentioning pregnancy and giving birth. So mentioning "the woman" is more appropriate for it, because the quality of femininity (unutha) is what necessitates conception and delivery, not insofar as she is a wife.

I say: It could be said that the secret in mentioning the believers and their women with the word "spouses" (azwaj) is that this word indicates similarity, kinship, and association, as is understood from its form. The two spouses (zawjan) are two things that are alike, resembling one another, or equal. From this is His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22].

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Their spouses" means their likenesses and their equals.

Imam Ahmad also said this.

(Section)

He said in (Zad al-Muhajir):

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Ibrahim? When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, [you are] a people unknown." Then he turned quickly to his family and brought a fatted calf, and placed it before them. He said, "Will you not eat?" And he felt apprehension of them. They said, "Do not fear," and gave him good tidings of a knowing boy. Then his wife came forward in a loud cry and struck her face and said, "An old barren woman!" They said, "Thus said your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾

So my counsel to you is that when you recite this verse, and look toward its meaning and reflect upon it, you will only perceive from it that the angels came to Ibrahim in the form of guests, eating and drinking, and gave him good tidings of a knowing boy. His wife was astonished at this, so the angels informed her that Allah had said this.

Your reflection does not go beyond this.

Now listen to some of what these verses contain of kinds of secrets.

How much they include of praise for Ibrahim.

How they combined hospitality and its rights.

What they include of refutation of the people of falsehood, from the philosophers and the Mu'attilah (those who deny the divine attributes).

How they include a great sign of the signs of prophethood.

How they include all the attributes of perfection, which they trace back to knowledge and wisdom.

How they include the report of the Lord's justice and His retribution upon the nations that denied.

They include mention of Islam and faith and the difference between them. They include the continuance of the signs of the Lord that indicate His oneness, the truthfulness of His messengers, and the Last Day.

They include that none benefits from all this except one in whose heart there is fear of the punishment of the Hereafter, and these are the believers in it.

As for one who does not fear the Hereafter and does not believe in it, he does not benefit from those signs.

Now listen to some details of this summary. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Ibrahim?﴾

He, glory be to Him, opened the story with a form that is designed for interrogation, and it is not meant in its literal sense as a question. For this reason some people said that "hal" in such a place means "qad," which implies confirmation. But there is a subtle secret and a wondrous meaning in the discourse coming in such a form of interrogation. When the speaker wants to inform the addressee of a strange matter that deserves attention, and to bring it to mind, he begins his speech with an interrogative particle, to alert his hearing and mind to what he is about to report. Sometimes he begins with "alā" and sometimes with "hal." So one says, "Do you know what happened, such and such?" Either to remind him of it, or to warn him, or to draw attention to the greatness of what is being reported, or to confirm it for him.

So His saying, ﴿Has there come to you the story of Musa?﴾ and ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ and ﴿Has there come to you the story of the Overwhelming?﴾ and ﴿Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Ibrahim?﴾ includes the glorification of these stories and the drawing of attention to contemplating them and understanding what they contain.

There is also another matter in it, which is an indication that the coming of this to you is one of the signs of prophethood, for it is of the unseen which neither you nor your people know. So has it come to you without Our informing you, sending you, and making you aware? Or has it not come to you except from Us? Observe how this discourse appears in the form of interrogation, and consider the great effect of its placement in all its occurrences; it testifies that it is at the summit of eloquence.

His saying ﴿the guests of Ibrahim, the honored ones﴾ includes praise of His intimate friend Ibrahim, for there are two opinions regarding "the honored ones."

The first: that Ibrahim honored them, and in this there is praise of Ibrahim for honoring the guest.

The second: that they are honored with Allah, as in His saying ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾. This also includes the glorification and praise of His intimate friend, since He made His honored angels guests of his. So on both interpretations there is praise of Ibrahim.

His saying ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ includes another praise of Ibrahim, in that he returned their greeting in a better form than the one in which they greeted him. Their greeting was with a noun in the accusative, which implies a verbal sentence; its estimated meaning is "We greet you with peace." Ibrahim's greeting to them was with a noun in the nominative, which implies a nominal sentence; its estimated meaning is "Peace be upon you, lasting, or established, or settled." There is no doubt that a nominal sentence indicates stability and permanence, while a verbal sentence indicates renewal and occurrence. So Ibrahim's greeting was more perfect and better.

Then He said ﴿a people unknown﴾.

In this, regarding the good manner in addressing a guest and the avoidance of harming him, there are two aspects of praise.

The first: he omitted the subject, the estimated meaning being "You are a people unknown," so he avoided them and did not address them with this speech, because of what it contains of causing unease.

The Prophet (ﷺ) would not confront anyone with what he disliked, but would say: "What is the matter with people who say such and such and do such and such?"

The second: his saying ﴿a people unknown﴾, in which he omitted the agent of the denial, who was the one who had denied them, as He said in another place "he denied them." There is no doubt that his saying "unknown" (munkarun) is gentler than saying "I deny you."

His saying ﴿Then he turned quickly to his family and brought a fatted calf and placed it before them. He said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ includes several aspects of praise and etiquettes of hospitality and honoring the guest.

Among them is His saying ﴿Then he turned quickly to his family﴾. "Ruwan" means to go away swiftly and secretly, and it includes hastening to honor the guest. And the secrecy includes avoiding embarrassing him and not presenting him to shame. This is unlike one who is sluggish and slow toward his guest, then appears in front of him, unties his purse of expenses, weighs what he takes, and takes the vessel in front of him, and similar things that include embarrassing the guest and causing him shame.

So the word "rāgha" negates these two matters.

In His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿to his family﴾ there is another praise, for it indicates that the honoring of the guest was ready and available with his family, and that he did not need to borrow from his neighbors, nor go to others than his household, since the provision for the guest was already present with them.

His saying ﴿and brought a fatted calf﴾ includes three kinds of praise:

The first: serving his guest himself, for he did not send it by another, but brought it himself.

The second: he brought them a whole animal, not part of it, so that they might choose from its best meat whatever they wished.

The third: it was fat, not lean, and this is among the choicest of wealth, a fat calf, which people admire. So from his generosity, slaughtering and presenting it was easy for him.

His saying ﴿before them﴾ includes praise and other etiquettes, which is bringing the food before the guest's presence, unlike one who prepares the food in one place and then seats his guest and brings it to him.

His saying ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ includes praise and further etiquettes, for he offered them food by saying ﴿Will you not eat?﴾. This is a form of offering that indicates gentleness, unlike one who says, "Put your hands to the food, eat, go ahead," and similar expressions.

His saying ﴿And he felt apprehension of them﴾: because when he saw that they were not eating from his food, he concealed within himself fear of them, lest they harbor evil. For when a guest eats from the food of the host, he feels secure with him and at ease. So when they realized this from him, they said ﴿Do not fear﴾ and ﴿gave him good tidings of a knowing boy﴾. This boy was Ishaq, not Isma'il, because his wife was astonished at this and said, "An old barren woman; I shall not bear a child, so how can I have a child?" As for Isma'il, he was from his concubine Hajar and was his firstborn and first child. Allah, may He be exalted, has explained this in Surat Hud in His saying ﴿So We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾, and this is the same story itself.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry and struck her face and said, "An old barren woman!"﴾ indicates the weakness of the woman's reason and the lack of her steadfastness, since she hastened to lamentation and struck her face at this news.

His saying ﴿An old barren woman﴾ indicates the good manners of a woman when addressing men, and her limiting of speech to what fulfills the need. For she omitted the subject and did not say, "I am an old barren woman," and she limited herself to mentioning the cause that indicates no childbirth, and mentioned nothing else. As for Surat Hud, she mentioned the cause that prevented it both for her and for Ibrahim, and she openly expressed astonishment.

His saying ﴿They said, "Thus says your Lord"﴾ includes the affirmation of the attribute of speech for Him. And His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ includes the affirmation of the attributes of wisdom and knowledge, which are the source of creation and command. So everything He created proceeds from His knowledge and wisdom, and likewise His command and legislation proceed from His knowledge and wisdom.

Knowledge and wisdom include all the attributes of perfection. Knowledge includes life and its necessary perfections: self-subsistence, power, permanence, hearing, sight, and the rest of the attributes that complete knowledge requires. Wisdom includes perfection of will, justice, mercy, benevolence, generosity, and goodness, the placing of things in their proper places in the best of their forms, and it includes the sending of messengers and the establishment of reward and punishment.

All of this is from His name al-Hakim, as is the method of the Qur'an in establishing these great matters through the attribute of wisdom, and in refuting those who claim that He created creation in vain, purposeless, and without truth. Thus the attribute of His wisdom includes the legislation, the decree, reward, and punishment. For this reason, the more correct of the two opinions is that the return (ma'ad) is known by reason, and that revelation came with the details of what reason indicates.

Whoever reflects on the method of the Qur'an will find it indicating this. He, glory be to Him, sets forth for them rational examples that show the possibility of the return at one time and its occurrence at another. He mentions the proofs of power that indicate the possibility of the return, and the proofs of wisdom that necessitate its occurrence.

Whoever reflects on the proofs of the return in the Qur'an will find them likewise, by the praise of Allah, sufficient in themselves without need of others, adequate and healing, leading to the sought goal swiftly, and including the answer to the doubts that occur to many people.

If success is granted, I would write a great volume on this, given what I have seen in the proofs to which the Qur'an guides, of healing and guidance, swiftness in bringing about conviction, excellence of explanation, and drawing attention to the places of doubt and answering them in a way that soothes the breast and increases certainty. This differs from other proofs, which are the reverse of that. But this is not the place for detail.

The purpose is that the emergence of creation and command proceeds from the knowledge and wisdom of the Lord.

This story was singled out for mention of these two names, because they imply the wonder of souls at the birth of a child between two parents who ordinarily cannot have children, and the obscurity of knowledge regarding the cause of this begetting, and the fact that wisdom required this birth to occur contrary to the known custom. So the verse mentions the name of Knowledge and Wisdom, which includes His knowledge of the cause of this creation, its purpose, and His wisdom in placing it in its proper place without violating the requirement of wisdom.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 51, verses 31–37:

Then the Exalted and Glorified mentioned the story of the angels in their being sent to destroy the people of Lut, and the sending of the stones marked (al-hijarah al-musawwamah) upon them.

In this is what contains the confirmation of His messengers, the destruction of those who denied them, and an indication of the Return (al-ma'ad) and of reward and punishment, since it occurred before the eyes in this world. This is among the greatest proofs indicating the truthfulness of His messengers, given the soundness of what they reported about their Lord.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers. But We found not in it except one house of Muslims.﴾

Here He distinguished between Islam and iman (faith) for a secret that the context required. The bringing out here is an expression for salvation, a bringing out of salvation from the punishment, and there is no doubt that this is specific to the believers who follow the messengers outwardly and inwardly.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But We found not in it except one house of Muslims.﴾

Since those who were found among those brought out, He applied the name of Islam to them, because the wife of Lut was from the people of this house and she was a Muslim outwardly. So she was among the house's occupants, not among the people who were saved.

Allah the Exalted has informed us of the betrayal of Lut's wife, and her betrayal was that she used to direct her people to his guests while her heart was with them. It was not a gross betrayal. So she was from the household that was Muslim outwardly, and not from the believers who were saved.

Whoever places the indications and wording of the Qur'an in their proper places will perceive from its secrets and wisdom what dazzles the minds, and will know that it is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.

With this, the answer to the well-known question is clear, which is: Islam is more general than iman, so how can the more general be excepted from the more specific? The rule of exception requires the reverse. This shows that the Muslims who were excepted are those upon whom the act of finding fell, while the believers were not excepted from it, but rather they are those brought out and saved.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾

In this is evidence that the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and His wonders which He performed in this world and whose traces He left, indicate Him and the truthfulness of His messengers, and only those who believe in the Return and fear the punishment of Allah benefit from them, as Allah the Exalted said in another place: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, and He the Exalted said: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾.

As for one who does not believe in the Hereafter, the most he will say is: "These are a people whom time befell, as it befell others, and time continues to hold misery and happiness." But whoever believes in the Hereafter and is apprehensive of it is the one who benefits from the signs and admonitions.

The purpose of this is merely to alert and to give an example of the differences in understanding in grasping the Qur'an and drawing out its secrets and the traces of its treasures, and that others may take a lesson from it. Bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers. But We found not in it except one house of Muslims.﴾

Here He distinguished between Islam and iman (faith) for a secret that the context required. The bringing out here is an expression for salvation, a bringing out of salvation from the punishment, and there is no doubt that this is specific to the believers who follow the messengers outwardly and inwardly.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But We found not in it except one house of Muslims.﴾

Since those who were found among those brought out, He applied the name of Islam to them, because the wife of Lut was from the people of this house and she was a Muslim outwardly. So she was among the house's occupants, not among the people who were saved.

Allah the Exalted has informed us of the betrayal of Lut's wife, and her betrayal was that she used to direct her people to his guests while her heart was with them. It was not a gross betrayal. So she was from the household that was Muslim outwardly, and not from the believers who were saved.

Whoever places the indications and wording of the Qur'an in their proper places will perceive from its secrets and wisdom what dazzles the minds, and will know that it is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.

With this, the answer to the well-known question is clear, which is: Islam is more general than iman, so how can the more general be excepted from the more specific? The rule of exception requires the reverse. This shows that the Muslims who were excepted are those upon whom the act of finding fell, while the believers were not excepted from it, but rather they are those brought out and saved.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾

In this is evidence that the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and His wonders which He performed in this world and whose traces He left, indicate Him and the truthfulness of His messengers, and only those who believe in the Return and fear the punishment of Allah benefit from them, as Allah the Exalted said in another place: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, and He the Exalted said: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾.

As for one who does not believe in the Hereafter, the most he will say is: "These are a people whom time befell, as it befell others, and time continues to hold misery and happiness." But whoever believes in the Hereafter and is apprehensive of it is the one who benefits from the signs and admonitions.

The purpose of this is merely to alert and to give an example of the differences in understanding in grasping the Qur'an and drawing out its secrets and the traces of its treasures, and that others may take a lesson from it. Bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills.

It is the one that does not fertilize, and there is no good in it, and the one that renders barren whatever it passes over.

The true monotheism (tawhid, the oneness of God) required of the servant is to flee from Allah to Allah.

In this phrase, the prepositions "min" (from) and "ila" (to) hold a great secret of tawhid. Fleeing to Him, glorified is He, entails singling Him out as the one sought and the one worshipped, along with what follows from that.

It therefore includes tawhid al-uluhiyya (the oneness of divinity and worship), on which the message of all the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all, agreed.

As for fleeing from Him to Him, it includes tawhid al-rububiyya (the oneness of lordship) and the affirmation of divine decree (qadar): that everything in the universe that is disliked and feared, from which the servant flees, has been brought into being solely by the will of Allah. What He wills comes to be and becomes necessary by His will, and what He does not will does not exist and its existence is impossible because He did not will it. So when the servant flees to Allah, he is fleeing from one thing to another thing that exists by the will and decree of Allah. In reality, then, he is fleeing from Allah to Him.

Whoever truly comprehends this understands the meaning of His (ﷺ) saying: "And I seek refuge in You from You," and his saying: "There is no refuge and no escape from You except to You." There is nothing in existence from which one flees, seeks refuge, or takes shelter except that it is from Allah, in its creation and origination. The one who flees and seeks refuge is fleeing from what the decree, will, and creation of Allah has brought into being, toward what His mercy, goodness, kindness, and benevolence require. So in reality he is fleeing from Allah to Him and seeking refuge in Allah from Him.

Grasping these two matters obliges the servant to sever the attachment of his heart to anything else completely, in fear, hope, and love. When he knows that what he flees from and seeks refuge from is only by the will, power, and creation of Allah, no fear remains in his heart of anyone other than its Creator and Originator. This entails singling out Allah alone for fear, love, and hope. If his fleeing were from something that was not by the will and power of Allah, that would necessitate fear of it, like someone who flees from one created being to another who is more powerful than him. In the state of fleeing from the first, he is afraid of it, fearing that the second will not protect him from it. By contrast, when the one to whom he flees is the One who decreed, measured, and willed what he flees from, no attention to anything else remains in the heart.

So reflect on this wondrous secret in the saying "I seek refuge in You from You" and "There is no refuge and no escape from You except to You." People have mentioned various views on this, and few have addressed this subtle point, which is the core and purpose of the speech. And with Allah is success.

Consider how the whole matter returns to fleeing from Allah to Him, which is the meaning of hijra (emigration) to Allah, the Exalted. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The emigrant is one who forsakes what Allah has forbidden."

For this reason Allah, glorified is He, joins faith and emigration in many places, because they are mutually necessitating and each requires the other.

The point is that emigration to Allah includes forsaking what He dislikes and doing what He loves and is pleased with. Its root is love and hatred, for the one who emigrates from one thing to another must find what he emigrates to more beloved than what he leaves, so he prefers the more beloved of the two over the other. The soul of the servant, his desire, and his Satan only call him to what is contrary to what Allah loves and is pleased with. He is afflicted with these three, and they never cease calling him to what does not please his Lord, while the caller of faith calls him to the pleasure of his Lord. So it is incumbent upon him at every moment to emigrate to Allah, and he should not cease in his emigration until death.

[Section: The Station of Fleeing]

Among the stations of "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" is the station of fleeing (firar).

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So flee to Allah﴾.

The reality of fleeing is escaping from one thing to another. It is of two kinds: the fleeing of the blessed and the fleeing of the wretched.

The fleeing of the blessed is fleeing to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The fleeing of the wretched is fleeing from Him, not to Him.

As for fleeing from Him to Him, this is the fleeing of His friends. Ibn Abbas said concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿So flee to Allah﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 50]: "Flee from Him to Him, and act in obedience to Him." Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: "Flee from what is other than Allah to Allah." Others said: "Flee from the punishment of Allah to His reward through faith and obedience."

The author of al-Manazil said: "It is escaping from what has not always existed to the One who has always existed." It has three levels: the fleeing of the common people from ignorance to knowledge in belief and in striving; from laziness to diligent exertion in earnest and resolve; and from constriction to expansiveness in trust and hope.

By "what has not always existed" he means creation, and by "what has always existed" he means the Truth.

As for his saying: "The fleeing of the common people from ignorance to knowledge in belief and striving":

Ignorance is of two kinds: lacking knowledge of the beneficial truth, and not acting in accordance with its requirement and demand. Both are ignorance linguistically, customarily, legally, and in reality. Moses said, ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqara: 67], when his people said to him, ﴿Do you make us a mockery?﴾, meaning, from among those who mock. Joseph the Truthful said, ﴿And unless You turn their plot away from me, I will incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 33], meaning, among those who commit what You have forbidden to them.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Repentance is only accepted by Allah from those who do wrong out of ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa: 17].

Qatada said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that everything by which Allah is disobeyed is ignorance." Others said: "The Companions agreed that everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant."

The poet said:

"Let none of us act ignorantly toward us, lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant."

The failure to observe knowledge is called ignorance, either because it is not benefited from, so it is treated as ignorance, or because of ignorance of the evil consequences that its actions bring about.

So the fleeing mentioned here is fleeing from both kinds of ignorance: from ignorance of knowledge to acquiring it, in belief, recognition, and insight; and from ignorance of action to beneficial striving and righteous deeds, with intention and effort.

As for his saying: "And from laziness to diligent exertion in earnest and resolve":

That is, one flees from answering the call of laziness to the call of action and exertion with earnestness and striving.

Earnestness (jidd) here is the sincerity of action and its purity from the taints of slackness and the promises of procrastination and negligence. Procrastination lies beneath the words "sin" (sawfa, "soon") , "perhaps" (asa), and "maybe" (la'alla). These are the most harmful things for the servant, and they are a tree whose fruit is loss and regret.

The difference between earnestness and resolve is that resolve is the sincerity and gathering of intention, while earnestness is the sincerity of action and the exertion of effort in it. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, commanded that His commands be received with resolve and earnestness. He said, ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqara: 63], and He said, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets an admonition about everything and an explanation of everything, so take them with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], and He said, ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12]. That is, with earnestness, striving, and resolve, not like one who takes what he is commanded with hesitation and slackness.

As for his saying: "And from constriction to expansiveness in trust and hope":

He means the servant's fleeing from the constriction of his chest caused by worries, griefs, sorrows, and fears that afflict him in this world, from himself, and from what is outside himself that relates to the means of his welfare, the welfare of those connected to him, and what relates to his wealth, body, family, and enemy. He flees from the constriction of his chest caused by all of that to the vast expanse of trust in Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, sincere reliance upon Him, good hope in His beautiful dealings with him, and expectation of what is hoped for from His kindness and goodness. Among the finest sayings of the common people is their saying: "There is no worry with Allah." Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2].

Al-Rabi ibn Khuthaym said: "He will make for him a way out from everything that is tight for people." Abu al-Aliya said: "A way out from every hardship." This comprehends the hardships and constrictions of this world and the Hereafter, for Allah makes for the one who fears Him a way out from everything that is tight and difficult for people in this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Hasan said: "A way out from what He has forbidden him." ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]: that is, He is sufficient for whoever trusts Him in his calamities and concerns. He suffices him for everything that troubles him. The "hasb" (sufficiency) is what is sufficient. ﴿Allah is sufficient for us﴾ means Allah suffices us.

Whenever the servant has good opinion of Allah, good hope in Him, and sincere reliance upon Him, Allah will never disappoint his hope in Him at all. He, glorified is He, does not disappoint the hope of one who hopes, nor does He waste the work of one who works. He expressed trust and good opinion with expansiveness, for there is nothing more expansive for the chest, nor more spacious, after faith than trust in Allah, hope in Him, and good opinion of Him.

(Section)

He said: "The fleeing of the elite is from report to witnessing, from outward forms to principles, and from portions to detachment (tajrid)."

He means that they are not content for their faith to be based only on report (khabar), but they seek to rise from it to witnessing what is reported, so they seek to ascend from the knowledge of certainty (ilm al-yaqin) through report to the sight of certainty (ayn al-yaqin) through witnessing, as Abraham the Friend, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, sought this from his Lord when he said, ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be satisfied"﴾ [al-Baqara: 260]. So Abraham sought that certainty become direct vision and the known become witnessed. This is the meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) expressed by doubt in his saying: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," since he said, ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾.

He (ﷺ) did not doubt, nor did Abraham; far be it from them both. He only expressed this meaning with this phrasing.

This is one of the opinions concerning the hadith.

There is a second opinion: that it is in the form of negation, meaning that Abraham did not doubt when he said what he said, and we do not doubt either. This view is also sound. That is, if what he sought had been out of doubt, we would have more right to it than he did. But he did not seek what he sought out of doubt; he sought it for reassurance.

The levels are three: the knowledge of certainty that comes from report; then the reality of what is reported becomes manifest to the heart or the eye, until knowledge of it becomes the sight of certainty; then one experiences and engages with it, and it becomes the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin). Our knowledge of Paradise and Hell now is knowledge of certainty. When Paradise is brought near to the righteous on the Standing, and Hellfire is displayed to the misguided, and they witness both directly, that is the sight of certainty, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire; then you will surely see it with the certainty of sight﴾ [al-Takathur: 6-7].

When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of Hell enter Hell, that is the truth of certainty. We will elaborate on this further, Allah willing, when we reach it.

(Section)

He said: "The fleeing of the elite of the elite is from what is beneath the Truth to the Truth, then from witnessing the fleeing to the Truth, then fleeing from witnessing the fleeing."

This is according to his principle of making annihilation from witnessing (fana' 'an al-shuhud) the ultimate goal of the wayfarers. First the servant flees from creation to the Truth, and through this flight he witnesses the singularity of the One he fled to. But a remnant remains in him, which is the witnessing of his own fleeing.

Then he becomes aware of creation again, so he flees a second time from the witnessing of his fleeing. Through this second flight all relations between him and creation are severed. Nothing remains in him except the observation of his fleeing from the witnessing of his fleeing, so he flees from the witnessing of fleeing, and then all relations are completely severed.

This has already been discussed, and it is not the highest of the stations and ranks, nor the ultimate perfection. Above it is what is higher in station and more noble in rank: that he witnesses his fleeing, and that he flees by Allah from Allah to Allah, so he witnesses that he fled by Him from Him to Him. He gives each station its right of servanthood. This is the state of the perfected, and Allah is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 51, verse 56:

He informed that He did not create the jinn and humankind out of any need of His for them, nor to profit from them. Rather, He created them out of generosity and benevolence, so that they would worship Him, and thereby they would gain every kind of profit from Him. This is like His saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls﴾ [Al-Isra: 7], and ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for their own souls that they prepare﴾ [Ar-Rum: 44].

(Section)

Know that He, glorified is He, must be worshipped with all kinds of worship ('ubudiyyah, servitude). Among the highest and most exalted of these is the worship of loyalty for His sake ('ubudiyyat al-muwalah fihi), enmity for His sake (al-mu'adah fihi), love for His sake (al-hubb fihi), hatred for His sake (al-bughd fihi), striving in His cause (al-jihad fi sabilihi), expending the lives of souls in seeking His pleasure, and opposing His enemies.

This kind is the summit of the hump of worship and its highest rank. It is the most beloved of its kinds to Him, and it depends upon what cannot be realized without it: the creation of souls that are loyal to Him, thankful to Him, and believe in Him, and of souls that are hostile to Him, disbelieve in Him, and whom He empowers over one another, so that His loves are realized in the most complete forms, His friends draw near to Him by striving against His enemies, opposing them, humbling and subduing them, and opposing their way. Thus His word and His call rise above the word and call of falsehood, and the nobility of its elevation and manifestation becomes clear. Had falsehood, disbelief and polytheism had no actual existence, then whatever His word and call were, they would rise, for elevation is a matter relative to something, which generally requires that which is elevated above.

The elevation of a thing over itself is impossible, and standing against a thing cannot be realized without it. This is clarified by the fact that among the worship of Him are freeing slaves, giving charity, preferring others over oneself, consoling and aiding others, pardoning, forgiving, patience, restraining anger, bearing hardships, and the like, all of which cannot be completed except by the existence of their object and their causes. Were it not for slavery, the worship of freeing slaves would not be realized, for enslavement is a consequence of disbelief. Were it not for injustice, transgression and aggression, the worship of patience, forgiveness and restraining anger would not be realized.

Were it not for poverty and need, the worship of charity, preferring others, and consoling others would not be realized. So if He had made all His creatures equal, these acts of worship, which are the most beloved thing to Him, would be nullified. For their sake He created the jinn and humankind, for their sake He legislated the laws, sent down the scriptures, sent the messengers, and created this world and the Hereafter. Just as that is among the attributes of His perfection, if He had not decreed the causes by which that is realized, this perfection would be absent, and the rulings of those attributes would be nullified.
